1 Overview

PULSAR is a desktop application for characterizing neural‑stimulation microelectrodes on the bench. It drives a Plexon PlexStim 2.0 electrical stimulator and a Tektronix TBS‑series oscilloscope — both over USB — to deliver precisely programmed current pulses and record the electrode's voltage response, then extracts the standard electrochemical safety and performance metrics: access voltage and resistance (Va / Ra), driving voltage (Vd), electrode polarization (Emc / Ema), charge per phase (Qph), and the headline result — the electrode's maximum charge‑injection capacity (max Qinj). It follows the protocols established for characterizing stimulation electrodes in the literature (Cogan 2008; Nguyen et al.).

POLARIS is the companion session viewer. It opens the data files PULSAR saves — and external PicoScope captures — so you can review waveforms, inspect and edit metrics, overlay a channel's captures, and export figures, all without any hardware attached. PULSAR is the instrument that acquires; POLARIS is the tool you use afterward to read.

Two names, one toolset. PULSAR is the acquisition GUI and POLARIS is the offline viewer. For historical reasons the installed program folder, the Windows executables (StimulationTesting.exe / StimulationTestingViewer.exe), and the settings folder still carry the original project name StimulationTesting. The Start Menu shortcuts and everything you see on screen use the PULSAR / POLARIS branding — they are the same software.

1.1  The measure → extract pipeline

Every experiment follows the same core loop. You author a stimulation pulse pattern (amplitude, phase widths, delays, shape), select which electrode site or multipolar combination to test, and press Start. For each capture PULSAR:

  1. Programs the pattern onto the stimulator and delivers it to the selected electrode site.
  2. Records the response on the oscilloscope. In AVERAGE mode the scope stacks many sweeps into one clean, low‑noise trace of the electrode voltage against time.
  3. Auto‑scales each scope channel's vertical range and position so the waveform fills the screen without clipping — you never touch the scope's front panel during a run.
  4. Extracts the metrics from the captured waveform and shows them, with markers on the plot and numbers in a side table, the instant the capture completes.
  5. Saves the raw waveforms, the computed metrics, and a full snapshot of the setup into a self‑describing session file, then auto‑exports a per‑channel figure and a metric workbook.

The signal PULSAR reads is the stimulator's own monitor outputs — a scaled copy of the voltage across the electrode (Vmon) and of the delivered current (Imon) — plus, when an instrumentation amplifier is wired into the bench, the individual electrode potentials (Eact / Eret) measured against a reference electrode. From these it computes the ohmic (IR) access drop, the interface polarization with the IR removed, and the charge injected per phase — the quantities that determine whether a stimulation protocol stays inside the electrode's water window (the potential range within which it charges without irreversible electrolysis; Merrill et al. 2005).

1.2  The hardware it drives

InstrumentRole
Plexon PlexStim 2.0 stimulator (USB)Delivers the programmed current pulses to one electrode site (or multipolar combination) at a time, and provides the Vmon / Imon monitor outputs. Only one program may own the stimulator at a time — close Plexon's own Sim‑2 / Stim‑2 application first.
Tektronix TBS‑series oscilloscope (USB)The acquisition front end. PULSAR supports the TBS2000 / 2000B / 2000C, TBS1000 / 1000B / 1000C, and legacy TDS / TPS families, in 2‑ and 4‑channel variants. It auto‑detects the model, its SCPI command dialect, and its display geometry when you connect.
Instrumentation amplifier (optional, bench‑wired)When present, it presents the active and return electrode potentials (Eact / Eret) against a reference electrode on spare scope channels. On a 4‑channel scope you can record both; when only Eret is available, PULSAR can derive Eact as Vmon + Eret.
USB camera (optional)A live bench preview that each experiment can periodically snapshot and/or record to video during a run — useful documentation of the physical setup.

On a minimal 2‑channel scope you map only Vmon and Imon; PULSAR then triggers on the Imon current edge. With more channels a dedicated digital sync line from the stimulator gives the cleanest timing, and the instrumentation‑amp potentials can be captured directly.

1.3  Who it is for

PULSAR is bench instrument‑control software for a laboratory setup. It is built for electrophysiology and neural‑interface researchers who characterize stimulation microelectrode arrays — SIROF, PtIr, IrOx, and similar coatings — and need repeatable, protocol‑faithful measurements of charge‑injection capacity, access resistance, and polarization, together with the water‑window safety screening those measurements support (Cogan 2008; Merrill et al. 2005). No programming is required: the whole workflow — connect, configure, author a pattern, run, read — is driven from the graphical interface.

Runs offline. PULSAR reads and writes local data files and talks to USB‑attached instruments only. During normal operation it makes no outbound network connections. The single exception is the optional finish‑notification email/text, which reaches the network only when you have explicitly enabled and configured it.

1.4  Learn it with the built‑in simulator

You do not need any hardware to explore PULSAR. It ships with a fully synthetic stimulator and oscilloscope that produce realistic waveforms and metrics, so you can practice the entire connect‑author‑run‑read workflow, and generate real session files to open in POLARIS, on any PC.

Tip. Tick Use simulator on the connection panel (or launch with --simulate) to run without instruments. This is the fastest way to learn the workflow and to verify a data‑analysis pipeline before touching the bench.

1.5  How to use this manual

The sections that follow track the order of a real session. Sections 2–4 cover installation and connecting the instruments; Sections 5–6 cover configuring the electrode, oscilloscope, and pulse pattern; Sections 7–9 describe the pulse pattern, the experiment types, and how to run one; Section 10 explains how to read the live plot and metrics; Sections 11–12 cover stimulator verification and the output files. Section 13 is a complete guide to the POLARIS viewer, Section 14 is troubleshooting, and Section 15 is a glossary of every metric with its definition and the reference it comes from. If a term is unfamiliar the first time you meet it, the glossary is the place to look it up.

2 Electrochemical background & safety

PULSAR exists to answer one question about a stimulating microelectrode: how much charge can it inject per pulse before it drives the electrode–electrolyte interface outside its safe operating window? Understanding the small amount of electrochemistry below makes every metric, limit, and safety stop in the rest of this manual meaningful. For the full treatment see the review by Cogan (2008); the protocol-design perspective is Merrill, Bikson & Jefferys (2005).

2.1 How a microelectrode injects charge

When a current pulse is delivered, charge crosses the electrode–tissue boundary by two mechanisms [Merrill 2005], [Harris 2019]:

  • Capacitive (non-Faradaic) charging of the electrical double layer — no chemical reaction, fully reversible. This is the safe mechanism.
  • Faradaic reactions — electrons transfer to/from chemical species at the surface. Some are reversible (e.g. the valence changes of an iridium-oxide film), but others are irreversible (electrode corrosion, gas evolution, pH shifts) and damage the electrode or the surrounding tissue.

The total current is the sum of both, i = ic + if [Harris 2019]. Because the two cannot be separated from a single galvanostatic (constant-current) pulse, a voltage transient cannot yield a clean double-layer capacitance, and applying Ohm’s law to the polarization is not valid [Harris 2024]. This is why PULSAR reports voltages (access, driving, polarization) and a charge capacity rather than a pulse-derived capacitance — see the Glossary.

2.2 The water window

The water window is the range of electrode potential (measured against a reference such as Ag | AgCl) within which charge is injected reversibly — wide enough to charge the double layer and drive reversible Faradaic reactions, but not so wide that it electrolyses water. Beyond the cathodic limit the electrode reduces water and evolves hydrogen; beyond the anodic limit it oxidises water and evolves oxygen (and, for platinum, dissolves) [Cogan 2008]. For platinum in saline the window is roughly −0.6 V to +0.8 V vs Ag | AgCl — the default limits PULSAR ships with.

Why this is the central safety concept. Over-pulsing an electrode past its water window degrades it — for activated iridium oxide this has been shown directly [Cogan 2004]. PULSAR’s Voltage-Transient experiment ramps the current only until Emc (or Ema) reaches the limit, then stops — so it finds the maximum safe charge without crossing it.

2.3 Charge per phase, charge density, and the safety model

Two quantities set the injury risk of a pulse [McCreery 1990]:

  • Charge per phase (Qph) — the time-integral of the current over one phase (units: nC or µC/phase). PULSAR computes it from the ideal programmed waveform.
  • Charge density — charge per phase divided by the electrode’s surface area (µC/cm² or mC/cm²). The same charge is far more damaging through a small electrode.

Shannon (1992) combined the two into a single log–log safety boundary, log(D) = k − log(Q), where D is charge density and Q is charge per phase; the constant k separates safe from potentially-damaging stimulation (recent work extends this model across pH and materials [Niederhoffer 2024]). The practical figure of merit PULSAR reports is the maximum charge-injection capacity, max(Qinj) — the charge density at the largest current whose electrode polarization still sits inside the water window [Nguyen 2024]. Comparing that capacity across stimulation polarity, configuration, and pulse pattern is exactly what PULSAR is designed to automate [Nguyen 2025].

Order-of-magnitude charge-injection limits (per Cogan 2008; PULSAR does not assume these — it measures each electrode). Values depend heavily on pulse width, bias, and geometry.
CoatingApprox. safe charge-injection limit
Platinum / Pt-Ir~0.05–0.15 mC/cm²
Sputtered iridium oxide (SIROF)~1–3 mC/cm² [Negi 2010]
Activated iridium oxide (AIROF)~1–5 mC/cm² (bias-dependent) [Cogan 2005]
Titanium nitride (TiN)~0.9 mC/cm²

2.4 What PULSAR measures, and why voltages

From each averaged voltage transient PULSAR extracts (all defined in the plot & metrics and glossary sections): the access voltage / resistance (the instantaneous ohmic iR step at the current edge), the driving voltage (the total electrode-vs-return voltage the stimulator must supply), and the electrode polarization Emc / Ema (the excursions checked against the water window). These are reported as measured voltages precisely because a voltage transient does not permit a valid Ohm’s-law or capacitance decomposition [Harris 2024]. For continuous-sinusoidal (kilohertz, KHFAC) stimulation PULSAR instead uses the access-resistance / interface-potential decomposition of Ghazavi & Cogan (2018).

3 Installation & first launch

PULSAR is Windows desktop software. It is distributed as a single ZIP that contains the installer, this manual, and a short read-me. This section walks through unpacking that ZIP, running the installer (including in-place upgrades), clearing the expected SmartScreen / antivirus warning, and what happens the first time PULSAR runs — then explains the simulator and where every file the software touches actually lives.

3.1 What's in the download

The delivery is a single ZIP named PULSAR.zip. The name is deliberately version-less so the shared download link never changes between releases — the version lives inside, on the installer's filename and in the read-me. Unzip it to any folder (Downloads is fine) and you will find:

FileWhat it is
PULSAR-Setup-<version>.exeThe installer. The <version> in the filename tells you which build you have (e.g. PULSAR-Setup-0.2.167.exe).
PULSAR-POLARIS-Manual.htmlThis manual. Open it in any web browser; there is nothing to install. To make a printed copy, open it and use Ctrl+P → Save as PDF.
README.txtA one-page “read me first” with the quick-start steps and the installer's SHA-256 checksum.
Collaborator (CWRU) build. Some sites receive PULSAR-CWRU.zip instead, whose installer is named PULSAR-Setup-<version>-CWRU.exe. It is functionally the same application; it adds an extra PULSAR-CWRU-IT-whitelist-request.txt you can forward to your IT department (see 3.3).

3.2 Running the installer

  1. Close PULSAR and POLARIS if either is already running.
  2. Double-click PULSAR-Setup-<version>.exe. Windows will ask for administrator rights — the installer writes the program files under Program Files, which requires elevation. (Only the install needs admin; PULSAR itself never writes to Program Files at runtime.)
  3. Follow the wizard. Early on it shows a Required hardware drivers page that checks for NI-VISA (needed to talk to the Tektronix oscilloscope) and Plexon Stim-2 (needed for a real stimulator), marking each Installed or Not found. If a driver is missing it offers a link that downloads and runs that driver's installer for you. Both drivers require a reboot — the recommended order is: install the driver(s), restart Windows, then re-run this installer. Driver setup is covered in full in §4 Connecting hardware; you can also skip the drivers now and add them later if you only want to explore the app in the simulator.
  4. When the wizard finishes, launch PULSAR (and, when you want to review saved data, POLARIS) from the Start Menu.

Upgrading in place

Installing a newer build over an existing copy upgrades it in place — the same install folder, a single entry in Add / Remove Programs, no sibling copy. Your settings, stimulator calibration/verification, learned electrode potentials, and every saved session file are preserved across the upgrade (they live outside the program folder — see 3.6).

Before you upgrade. Close both PULSAR and POLARIS first. Files that are open or in use can't be replaced, and a stimulator/scope that is still claimed by a running copy will block the new one. No need to uninstall the old version — just run the new installer.

3.3 SmartScreen & antivirus (expected, and how to clear it)

PULSAR is an in-house research tool and is not yet code-signed, so Windows treats it as an unknown publisher with no download reputation. Two harmless-but-alarming things can happen:

“Windows protected your PC” (SmartScreen). A blue dialog appears when you run the installer. Click More info, then Run anyway. This is expected for a new unsigned build — it is not a virus.
Antivirus flags or quarantines the installer. PULSAR is packaged with PyInstaller, which bundles a Python runtime into a self-extracting .exe. That packaging pattern is a well-known source of heuristic false positives, independent of what the program does. If Windows Defender or your corporate AV blocks it outright, give your IT department the installer's SHA-256 and ask them to allow that specific file by hash.

The SHA-256 is printed in the bundled README.txt. You can verify your download matches it — open PowerShell in the folder and run:

Get-FileHash .\PULSAR-Setup-<version>.exe -Algorithm SHA256

The reported hash should equal the one in the read-me exactly (case-insensitive). If your ZIP is the CWRU build, the enclosed PULSAR-CWRU-IT-whitelist-request.txt is a ready-to-forward note for your IT / information- security team: it explains why the false positive occurs, states the security posture (the app controls USB-attached lab instruments and reads/writes local files only — during normal operation it makes no outbound network connections), and lists the file identifiers and SHA-256 for whitelisting.

The permanent fix is on the way. A code-signing certificate is being obtained through University of Utah IT. Once builds are signed, Windows can trust them by publisher and these warnings disappear.

3.4 First launch — the admin password

The very first time PULSAR runs, it shows a one-time “Set up admin password” dialog. The admin password protects one thing: the custom pulse-shape catalog (managing and unlocking restricted pulse shapes via Admin → Manage Custom Catalog). It does not gate everyday testing.

You have two choices in the dialog:

  • Set a password — type it twice (the fields must match) and press Save and continue.
  • Use default for now — accept the publicly-known factory default. The dialog won't nag again, but because the default is public you should change the password later when convenient.
You rarely need to log in. Running experiments — connecting hardware, authoring pulses, sweeping current, saving data — needs no login at all. You only log in (via Admin → Log In…) when you want to manage the custom shape catalog. To change the password at any time, use Admin → Manage Custom Catalog → Change password…

After the dialog, PULSAR opens on the Setup tab — the left-most workflow tab and the start of the Setup → Test parameters → experiment flow described in the following sections.

3.5 No hardware? Use the simulator

PULSAR runs end-to-end with no stimulator or oscilloscope attached, driving a synthetic stimulator and scope that produce realistic waveforms. This is the fastest way to learn the workflow, and it's how you can follow every screen in this manual at your desk.

  • On the Setup tab's connection controls, tick Use simulator, then press Initialize / Connect as usual — the indicators turn green against the simulated devices.
  • Or launch PULSAR from a command line with the --simulate flag to start in simulator mode.
Tip. Everything a real run produces — the live plot, metric markers, the metrics table, and the saved .npz / .xlsx / figure files — works identically in the simulator, so you can practice authoring patterns, running each experiment, and reading the output before touching the bench.

3.6 Where your files live

PULSAR keeps three kinds of files in three deliberately different places, so an uninstall or a wiped save folder never takes the wrong thing with it:

KindLocationNotes
Configuration & state — preferences, stimulator calibration/verification, learned electrode potentials%APPDATA%\StimulationTesting\Per-user, in your roaming profile. Files such as prefs.json, calibration.json, and electrode_potential_history.json. Survives uninstall and follows you across machines, which is why an upgrade keeps all your settings.
Session data — per-run capture data (.npz), the metric workbook (.xlsx), per-channel figures (.tif/.png/.svg), and the session log (.txt)The Save location you choose on the Setup tabYou pick this folder; the filename stem is notebook + session. An aborted run marks its files with an _ABORTED suffix so incomplete data is obvious.
Crash / launch error logs — a diagnostic written only if PULSAR fails to start (pulsar_launch_error.log)A writable spot next to the program / session files, or %USERPROFILE%\.stimtest\ as a fallbackNever in %APPDATA% or %TEMP%. On a standard Program Files install (read-only at runtime) these land in your home folder's .stimtest\.
Heads-up about OneDrive save locations. Saving inside a OneDrive-synced folder works, but OneDrive can briefly lock a file mid-write while it syncs — which can surface, intermittently, as an [WinError 5] Access is denied error exactly when PULSAR writes a .npz or .xlsx. If you hit that, simply retry the save, or point the Save location at a non-synced local folder (e.g. C:\PULSAR_data) to avoid it entirely. Configuration files in %APPDATA% are unaffected.

4 The PULSAR window

PULSAR is organized as one window with a menu bar across the top, a strip of workflow tabs just below it, and a shared log pane pinned to the bottom. You drive a session by moving left-to-right across the tabs: connect and configure on Setup, author the pulse on Test parameters, watch the run on the experiment tab, and revisit finished data on Results. A draggable splitter separates the tab area from the log, so you can pull the log taller whenever you want more history on screen.

4.1  The workflow tabs

The tab strip runs left to right in the order you use it. Only the experiment tab for the experiment you have selected is shown at any time — switching experiments swaps the tab in place, but each experiment tab keeps its own selected channels, parameters and captured data, so nothing is lost when you come back to it.

TabWhat you do there
SetupConnect the stimulator, oscilloscope and (optionally) a camera; choose the device/array, electrode coating and area; map oscilloscope channels; set acquisition & trigger; define the water-window limits; and pick where session files are saved. See §5 and §6.
Test parametersAuthor the stimulation pulse pattern and set the parameters for the selected experiment, then select the channel(s) or combination(s) to run. Hosts the live pulse preview. See §7.
Voltage Transient / Progressive Stress / Short-Term Pulsing / Continuous Pulsing / Long-Term Pulsing / Galvanostatic EIS The live experiment view — a scope plot with metric markers on the left and a metrics table on the right. Exactly one experiment tab is present at a time; it is titled for the experiment you chose. See §8.
ResultsAn embedded POLARIS viewer pointed at your save folder, for reviewing finished captures without leaving PULSAR. See §13.
VerificationAn optional tab that appears only when you start a stimulator verification — from Run → Stimulator Verification… or the Run Verification button on Setup. It slots in right after Setup. See §11.
The Start / Pause / Stop buttons follow you. The active experiment's run-control button row appears at the bottom of whichever tab you are on — Test parameters or the experiment view — so you can launch a run from either place. Clicking Start also auto-switches you from Test parameters to the experiment view so you can watch it. (Scrolling the mouse wheel over the tabs does not flip between them — that is deliberate, so an accidental scroll can't change tabs mid-run.)

4.2  The experiment view

Every experiment tab shares the same three-part layout, shown in the figure above:

  • Left — trace column and channel list. A checkbox per trace (Vmon, Imon, Eret, Eact, and their derived/overlay variants) with a small dropdown to place each on the left or right axis, above the list of channels/combinations being run. A Latest button jumps back to the most recent capture after you have paged through older ones.
  • Centre — the scope plot. The recorded traces with the metric markers drawn on them. PULSAR sizes each channel's vertical scale and position automatically, so you never touch the scope's front panel during a run. Reading the plot and markers is covered in §10.
  • Right — the metrics table. The numeric values for exactly the capture currently shown in the plot. Paging the plot to a different capture repoints the table to match, so the numbers and the waveform never disagree.

A thin run-progress bar sits above the plot while a run is live: it shows elapsed vs. total time for the duration-based experiments, and channel-step progress (for example channel 3/16) for the sweeping ones. Some experiments add extra sub-tabs here — for example a Tracking plot for Progressive Stress and Long-Term Pulsing, or Bode and Nyquist plots for Galvanostatic EIS.

4.3  The menu bar

Seven menus span the top of the window. Everything you need for a normal session is reachable from the tabs; the menus add shortcuts, session-wide settings and utilities.

File

ItemShortcutPurpose
Save settings…Ctrl+SSnapshot the full GUI state (every tab's parameters) to a named file, e.g. to keep a per-subject or per-array configuration.
Load settings…Ctrl+ORestore a previously saved settings file.
Reset to default—Return every tab to the values built into this version, and overwrite the auto-saved preferences so the reset sticks.
QuitCtrl+QClose PULSAR (your current settings are auto-saved on exit).
Your settings are remembered automatically. PULSAR saves your last-used values on close and again whenever you press Start, so the next launch comes up exactly where you left off. The File menu is for keeping named snapshots on top of that automatic behaviour.

Edit

Undo (Ctrl+Z), Redo (Ctrl+Y), Cut / Copy / Paste and Select All — the standard text-editing actions, applied to whichever input field, table cell or the log pane currently has focus.

Run

Stimulator Verification…—Open the Verification tab (enabled only once both the stimulator and oscilloscope are connected).
Open Viewer—Launch the standalone POLARIS session viewer.

The Start, Stop and Single capture entries are greyed out until a run is live — they mirror the in-tab button row, which also carries a Pause / Continue control (halts pulsing and holds, then resumes where it left off). Connection control is deliberately not in this menu: the stimulator has Initialize / Close and the scope has Connect / Disconnect, and those live on the Setup-tab connection panel (§5).

Theme. View → Theme switches the window chrome between Light, Dark and System (which follows your Windows colour-scheme setting and updates automatically if you change it). The choice is remembered between launches. Only the surrounding interface changes colour — the plots stay on a white background in every theme, deliberately, so they match the exported figures and stay legible for publication.

Admin

The Admin menu manages the login used to unlock the restricted (custom) pulse-shape catalog. Everyday testing needs no login. Log In… / Log Out switch profiles; Manage Custom Catalog… (visible only while logged in as administrator) edits the catalog; Import Profile… adds a profile file supplied by a collaborator (open to everyone — you still need its password to use it), and Export Profile… (administrator only) writes one out. The administrator password is set on first launch and can be changed here.

4.4  The log pane

The log pane along the bottom is shared by every tab, so a running commentary of the whole session is always in view. It records each setting you change (prefixed Setup:), each pattern edit, every hardware command and every run event, and it mirrors everything to the session .txt log on disk as it happens — so a completed run leaves a full text record next to its data files. It opens with a banner capturing the date, software versions and whether you are in live-hardware or simulator mode, which makes a saved log self-documenting for later review.

Long lines wrap with a hanging indent so they stay readable, and a small Go to latest line button appears in the corner whenever you have scrolled up, to jump back to the newest entry. Drag the splitter above the log to make it taller or shorter at any time.

The log is your first stop when something looks off. Because it is timestamped and saved to disk, you can reconstruct exactly what was configured and what the instruments did — invaluable when comparing a puzzling capture against a good one, or when reporting a problem.

4.5  Window title and the run lock

The title bar reads PULSAR followed by the version (for example PULSAR v0.2.167), so a bench screenshot or bug report always identifies the exact build. The companion session viewer runs in its own window whose title reads POLARIS — if you have both open, the title bar tells you which is which.

What locks while a run is live. Once you press Start, PULSAR guards against reconfiguring the experiment out from under itself, but keeps everything readable:
  • Setup and Test parameters stay selectable and scrollable — you can review any setting during a run — but their input controls grey out so nothing can be changed mid-run.
  • The Results tab is fully disabled, so opening a saved file can't collide with the live capture pipeline.
  • The experiment view keeps updating — its plot, markers and metrics table refresh with each capture, and the run-progress bar advances.
Values are snapshotted at Start, so any edit you make afterward is ignored for that run. When the run ends, the input controls unlock automatically.

5 Connecting hardware

The connection controls live at the top of the Setup tab.

4.1  Stimulator

Press Initialize. On success the indicator turns green and the serial number / firmware are shown.

“No Plexon Stimulator is detected.” Plexon's own Stim‑2 application holds an exclusive USB lock on the stimulator. Close it, then press Initialize again. Only one program can own the stimulator at a time — PULSAR also prevents a second PULSAR window from opening for the same reason.

4.2  Oscilloscope

Press Connect. PULSAR queries the model, probes its SCPI dialect, and reads the display geometry. It supports the TBS2000/2000B/2000C, TBS1000/1000B/1000C, and legacy TDS/TPS families (2‑ and 4‑channel).

USB “semaphore timeout” on connect? A previous PULSAR that crashed can leave the scope's USB endpoint claimed. PULSAR retries automatically (up to three times); if it still fails, power‑cycle the scope, replug the USB cable, and press Connect again.

4.3  Camera (optional)

If a USB camera is present, pick it in the Camera connector and press Connect. A live preview appears, and each experiment tab can periodically snapshot and/or record video of the bench during a run (configured on the Test‑parameters page). A prominent badge shows LIVE PREVIEW vs ● RECORDING so you never confuse the two.

6 Setup tab

The Setup tab is where you tell PULSAR everything about the physical test — which electrode you are characterizing, how it is wired to the stimulator, which oscilloscope channel carries which signal, how the scope acquires, where the electrochemical safety limits sit, and where the results are saved. PULSAR takes a snapshot of these values the moment you press Start, so getting them right here is the foundation of every run.

The tab is two columns. The left column is a scrollable stack of grouped forms — Hardware (connection panel, see §4), Session, Test device parameters, Oscilloscope channel mapping, Oscilloscope acquisition, and Experiment to run. The right column shows the selected device's electrode geometry and its editable channel grid, with the Cable channel mapping tree beneath it. During a run the left-column inputs are locked, but you can still scroll and read every setting.

Every change is logged. Each control you touch writes a line to the log pane at the bottom of the window (and to the session .txt log), so a run's provenance is fully recorded. Numeric fields commit when you press Enter or click out — not on every keystroke.

6.1 Session identity & file naming

The Session group holds the bookkeeping that names your files and records who ran the test.

FieldWhat it does
NotebookA project / notebook label prefixed onto every filename so a day's captures from different electrodes share a parent. Untick the Notebook: checkbox to drop the prefix (the log becomes <Session>_log.txt instead of <Notebook>_<Session>_log.txt).
SessionThe identifier for the electrode / sample under test. Suffixed onto the notebook to form the unique file stem (e.g. session_001_electrode_a1). Change this between electrodes so files don't overwrite each other.
User name / emailOperator provenance, recorded in every saved session. The email is also the recipient for finish notifications and the attribution if you opt in to contribute data.
User phone / CarrierOptional mobile number (digits only) and carrier for run-end text alerts, sent through your carrier's email-to-SMS gateway.
Institution / CompanyOptional affiliation, saved with your prefs; used as attribution if you contribute anonymised data.

6.2 Device & array

The Test device dropdown picks your electrode array. Selecting one auto-fills that device's recommended electrode area, default coating, and connector pinout — all of which you can still override below. The right-column panel then draws the array's geometry and its channel grid.

DeviceNotes
Plexon Test BoardA no-electrode verification board (see the no-electrode note below).
LinearSingle-column linear probe (the fresh-install default).
Blackrock Omnetics (4×4) / Blackrock PCB (4×4)16-channel Utah-style arrays.
MicroProbes 16-channel FMAFloating microelectrode array (triangular packing).
NeuroNexus A4×4 / UTD MEACatalogued research arrays.
Other (custom grid)Author your own mapping by hand; a Grid type chooser appears — Square (rectangular) or Hexagonal (triangular) — to tell PULSAR how the pads pack.

On the right, the device panel has a geometry visualizer (one disk per channel, numbered) beside an editable channel-map table. Use the Rows / Cols spinboxes to resize a custom grid; type a channel number into a cell (or 0/blank for an empty site, shown as a dim “—”). You can paste a whole block copied from a spreadsheet.

The Plexon Test Board is a no-electrode device. When it is selected, PULSAR hides the electrode options (coating, surface area, geometry, return / reference electrode) because the board has no electrodes, and it disables area-normalized metrics — charge-injection density (mC/cm2) and current density are reported as raw charge / current instead. The scope-mapping dropdowns also drop Eret and Eact (only Vmon / Imon / Trigger / None remain), and the plot voltage axis stays the plain Voltage [V]. Switching back to a real array restores all of these — including your previous scope-channel choices.

6.3 Coating, surface area & geometry

  • Active / working electrode — the electrode material (SIROF, AIROF, TiN, Pt, PtIr, PEDOT:PSS, Au, W, …). Selecting a coating auto-fills the cathodic / anodic potential limits below from the catalog values for that material. Choose Custom… to type a material not in the catalog (the limits then stay at whatever you have typed). One coating applies to the whole array.
  • Surface area — the geometric surface area of one electrode pad, entered as a value plus a unit (µm², mm², or cm²; switching units rescales the number so the physical area is unchanged). This converts charge to charge density (mC/cm2) and current to current density. Untick Same for all to expose a per-channel area column in the device-view table for arrays with mixed pad sizes.
  • Electrode geometry — the pad shape (circle, square, rectangle, cone, ring, band), which sets the geometric-surface-area formula. The Rounded toggle (filleted corners / pill cap) appears only for the square and rectangle geometries.

6.4 Return & reference electrode

PULSAR distinguishes the return / counter electrode (which carries the return current) from the reference electrode (the third terminal in a 3-electrode cell, against which potentials are quoted).

  • Return / counter electrode — tick this when a separate return electrode is used (e.g. a Pt wire in the bath) instead of routing return through an on-array channel; the dropdown picks its material (Pt by default). A small readout shows that material's estimated open-circuit potential vs Ag|AgCl (an in-vitro / saline value; in an animal all counter potentials collapse to ≈ 0 V). Pick Custom to type an out-of-catalog material and its OCP.
  • Reference electrode — on by default, defaulting to Ag|AgCl (0 V shift, so the displayed limits equal the catalog numbers). Selecting a different reference subtracts that material's OCP vs Ag|AgCl, re-expressing the cathodic / anodic limits as V vs <your reference>. Untick to interpret the limits as V vs Ag|AgCl by convention. When the reference is off but a return electrode is set, the return material acts as the reference baseline for the limit shift.
Remembered open-circuit potential is a recommendation, never applied. The Remember return-electrode potential toggle (on by default) records each finished capture's measured Eret rest potential into a per-coating learned store. That measured value is surfaced only as a · tested +0.217 ± 0.012 V annotation next to the reference / return readout — it never overrides your set water-window limits. Turn the toggle off to stop recording; clear the store from Help → Reset learned electrode potentials… if early data contaminated it.

6.5 Cable channel mapping

The Cable dropdown (directly under the device) and the Cable channel mapping tree on the right together describe how each device channel you select is wired to a Plexon stimulator channel. This is a pure channel-number translation: you select, capture, plot, and label everything by the device channel, while PULSAR issues every stimulator command to the Plexon channel the cable routes it to.

CableMapping
Omnetics UTDIdentity — pin N drives device CH N.
Omnetics NNXNeuroNexus re-order.
Plexon (UTD)PlexStim port order (device CH01 → Plexon CH15, etc.).
2×8 Pin Receptacle / Large Black OmneticsStraight-through (identity); the two cables offered for the Plexon Test Board.
Plexon Omnetics8-channel bank swap (device CH09 → Plexon CH01, etc.).
CustomEdit the pin map yourself — see below.

The tree lists one row per channel: column 1 is the Device channel you see, column 2 is the Plexon channel PULSAR actually commands. Rows where the two differ are shown in bold, and the header notes whether the cable is (identity) or (N re-mapped). Choosing the Custom cable makes column 2 double-click-editable — type each device channel's Plexon channel (1–16); the map stays a permutation, so editing one row swaps it with whichever row held that channel. Custom maps persist between sessions.

Verify at Start. The active translation is written to the log at the start of every run (e.g. Cable translation ACTIVE — device:Plexon = 1:15, 2:13, …, or identity — no remap), so you can confirm a pulse on device CHnn reaches the port you intend.

6.6 Oscilloscope channel → role mapping

The Oscilloscope channel mapping group assigns a role to each physical scope channel (CH1–CH4). Each row has a role dropdown plus per-channel Bandwidth and Coupling overrides (§6.7).

RoleMeaning
VmonVoltage monitor — the voltage across the electrode (active vs return).
ImonCurrent monitor — the delivered stimulus current.
EretReturn-electrode potential vs reference, when instrumented.
EactActive-electrode potential vs reference, when instrumented. If Eret is recorded, Eact can be derived as Vmon + Eret.
TriggerA digital sync line from the stimulator (the preferred trigger source).
NoneChannel unused.

On a fresh install the first scope connect applies the catalog default (CH1 = Vmon, CH2 = Imon, CH3 = Eret, CH4 = Eact). After that, your assignments are remembered — including a deliberate None — and survive disconnect, reconnect, and restart. On a 2-channel scope the CH3/CH4 rows are hidden, but their stored roles are preserved for when a 4-channel scope reconnects.

Trigger source. A channel with the Trigger role (a Plexon digital sync wired to it) gives the cleanest timing. If no channel is set to Trigger, PULSAR falls back to triggering on the Imon current edge — which works for normal pulses but requires a non-zero stimulus current, so a digital Trigger is preferable when available.

6.7 Per-channel bandwidth & coupling

Each scope-channel row also carries a Bandwidth and a Coupling dropdown, in line with the role. Both default to Auto, which applies PULSAR's automatic policy; a concrete choice overrides it for that channel. (These dropdowns are disabled when the channel's role is None.)

DropdownOptions
BandwidthAuto — full bandwidth on data channels, 20 MHz on the trigger channel for a clean comparator. Full — maximum edge detail. 20 MHz — band-limit a noisy channel.
CouplingAuto — DC for the monitors and electrodes, AC for a distinct digital trigger. DC / AC — force that coupling. DC + AC — capture once in DC to read the rest potential, then AC-couple so the small pulse swing fine-scales, and sum the DC offset back in. This is intended for a DC-biased electrode (e.g. a monopolar Eret) and applies during a Voltage-Transient run.
Leave both on Auto unless you have a specific reason. The automatic policy already band-limits the trigger, DC-couples the monitors, and — when there is no dedicated Trigger channel — locks the Imon channel to 20 MHz (so its edge reliably fires the scope).

6.8 Acquisition & trigger

The Oscilloscope acquisition group controls how the scope samples each capture.

  • Mode — AVERAGE (recommended) coherently averages several sweeps for a much lower noise floor; SAMPLE captures each trigger as-is.
  • Average count — an up/down spinbox (its range set from the connected scope model). When you commit a value PULSAR writes it to the scope and reads it back; Tektronix snaps the count to its supported power-of-two grid, and the field is updated to the confirmed value so what you see is what the scope will actually average.
  • Horizontal window — Wide (default) frames a wider time window with more post-pulse recovery; Tight makes the pulse fill more of the screen. The scope's timebase grid is coarse, so the two modes pick different steps (e.g. a 400 µs biphasic → 1500 µs Wide vs 600 µs Tight on a TBS2204B).
  • Use digital sync trigger (EXT) — appears only when the connected scope has an external trigger input; check it to trigger off the Plexon digital sync wired to the EXT BNC, uncheck to use the Imon fallback.

An approximate acquisition time per capture (average count ÷ pulse rate) is shown on the Test parameters page next to the pulse-rate control, so you can gauge how long each capture will take before you start.

6.9 Water-window potential limits

The Potential limits row sets the electrochemical safety boundary — the cathodic limit (Elc, default −0.6 V), the anodic limit (Ela, default +0.8 V), and a tolerance (± grace band, default 0.020 V). These pre-fill from the selected coating's catalog values but are fully editable per session. PULSAR uses them to bound the adaptive Voltage-Transient ramp: it stops raising the current once the electrode polarization reaches the limit band, so it finds the maximum safe charge injection without driving the electrode past its water window Cogan 2008.

When a non-Ag|AgCl reference has shifted the displayed limits (§6.4), a small italic line under each limit shows its original vs-Ag|AgCl value and the shift applied, so you can always read both scales.

You own these values. The water-window limits are the safety boundary for your electrode material and reference. PULSAR will not knowingly ramp past them, but it cannot verify that the numbers are correct — set them deliberately for your chemistry.

Context Two further rows — Environment (PBS, tissue, cell culture, …) and Gas sparging — record the electrolyte and atmosphere. They are metadata that also tune the pre-run damage-screen posture; they do not change what is delivered.

6.10 Saving & notifications

The Save path field (with a Browse… button) sets the folder where session files are written. The path must be an existing, writable folder: if it isn't, the field is outlined in red and the save-related options are disabled until you pick a real folder — this prevents a typo from silently creating a stray directory. The saved file stem is the notebook + session name (§6.1).

OptionWhat it does
Save .xlsx after sessionAlso writes a Gamry-DTA-style workbook next to the .npz after each run (off by default; the .npz is always written).
Save plots during sessionWrites each channel/combo's figure next to the .npz in real time as that channel completes. Choose the format (PNG / JPEG / TIF / SVG — default TIF) and, for raster formats, the DPI (300 / 600 / 900 / 1200 — default 600; disabled for vector SVG).
Notify on finish (email / text)At the end of every run (success or failure) emails the User email and/or texts the User phone (if a carrier is set). Requires SMTP credentials configured on the machine (environment variables or ~/.stimtest/email_config.json); off by default.
OneDrive save locations. Saving experiment data inside OneDrive works, but OneDrive can briefly lock files mid-write, which occasionally surfaces as an “Access is denied” error when saving. If that happens, retry — or choose a non-synced local folder (e.g. C:\PULSAR_data) to sidestep it. PULSAR also logs a one-line notice when your Save location is inside OneDrive, as a reminder.

6.11 Experiment to run

The Experiment to run group picks which experiment the Test-parameters page and the live view are configured for (Voltage Transient, Progressive Stress, Short / Continuous / Long Pulsing, Galvanostatic EIS — see §7). A one-line blurb describes the current choice, and Go to test parameters tab → jumps you straight to authoring the pulse pattern for it.

7 Pulse pattern (Test parameters)

The Test parameters tab is where you author the current waveform that the stimulator delivers on every cycle. The pattern panel builds the shape phase-by-phase; a live preview redraws as you type, and a running charge summary tells you what will actually be injected. The same pattern feeds whichever experiment tab is active — you author it once, then pick channels and press Start.

A stimulus pulse is a sequence of phases (a constant-polarity segment of current) separated by optional zero-current delays, and the whole pulse repeats at the rate. Figure — names every part of a charge-balanced biphasic pulse — the anatomy the rest of this section refers back to.

7.1 Phase count, symmetry & polarity

Three top controls set the overall structure of the pulse:

  • Phase count — Biphasic (two phases, the usual case), Triphasic (three phases), or Arbitrary (a free-form table of amplitude / duration rows for special waveforms).
  • Symmetry (biphasic only) — Symmetric derives the second phase by mirroring the first, so you set one amplitude and one width; Asymmetric exposes an independent amplitude and width for every phase.
  • Polarity — Cathodal-first (the leading phase drives current out of the electrode; the default and the norm for neural stimulation) or Anodal-first. The polarity sets the sign of the excitation phase.
Cathodal-first vs. anodal-first. Polarity names which phase leads in time — the -al ending. The direction the electrode potential is then driven is described with the -ic ending: a cathodal-first pulse drives the electrode through its cathodic excursion first. Cathodal-first is standard because it recruits neurons at a lower threshold before the reversal phase recovers the charge Merrill 2005.

In Symmetric Triphasic mode a Triphasic ratio (a : b : c) row appears — three amplitude magnitudes, default 2 : 3 : 1 (the IEEE NER convention, with the largest-magnitude phase as the excitation phase). The sign of each phase alternates from the chosen polarity.

7.2 Amplitude, width & current resolution

Each phase carries an amplitude (µA) and a width (µs). The excitation phase — the largest-magnitude phase — displays its amplitude with the polarity sign, including an explicit leading +: a cathodal-first pulse reads -50.0 µA, an anodal-first pulse reads +50.0 µA, so the sign on screen always matches the polarity dropdown. Type a bare magnitude and the panel applies the correct sign automatically.

Amplitude and time both land on the PlexStim 2.0 hardware grids:

QuantityResolutionWhy
Time (phase width, delays)1 µsThe device's timing quantum. Widths are typed to whole microseconds.
Current — rectangular phase0.1 µA (100 nA)The grid the lab trusts the stimulator to deliver cleanly for a flat-top pulse.
Current — shaped phase30 nAThe PlexStim's native resolution — used only for non-rectangular phases so the curve renders smoothly.

The resolution is chosen per phase, by its shape: a rectangular cathodal phase paired with an exp-decay anodal recharge still snaps the rectangle to 0.1 µA while the curve uses 30 nA. An amplitude below the applicable grid (that isn't exactly zero) is rejected before the pattern is sent to the device, so a value can never be silently rounded away.

Zero current + Imon trigger. If the oscilloscope is triggered on the current monitor (the fallback used when no digital sync channel is mapped, e.g. a 2-channel scope), the excitation amplitude cannot be 0 µA — there would be no edge to trigger on. The panel clamps a 0 µA entry to ±0.1 µA (polarity-correct). With a dedicated digital Trigger channel this restriction does not apply, so a Voltage-Transient ramp can legitimately start from 0 µA.

7.3 Pulse shapes

Every phase can carry a shape — the contour the current follows across the phase width. Rectangular is the default; the other shapes trade peak-for-peak charge efficiency and are chosen from a dropdown that shows a small icon of each. The full catalogue:

ShapeContour across the phase
 RectangularConstant current for the whole width (the flat-top pulse).
 Linear increasing / decreasingA straight ramp from 0 up to the peak, or from the peak down to 0.
 Linear increasing → decreasing / decreasing → increasing Biphasic pairs that use mirrored ramp shapes on the two phases (one amplitude + one width, symmetric).
 SinusoidalA half-sine — zero at both ends, peak at the middle.
 GaussianA bell centred in the phase (σ = W/5), tapered to zero at both ends — one of the more charge-efficient monophasic shapes.
 Exponential increasing / decreasingA rising or decaying exponential across the phase.
 Exponential increasing → decreasing / decreasing → increasing Mirror-symmetric exponential pairs (a rising phase paired with a decaying phase at equal charge).

Whatever the shape, it fills the same phase envelope: the width and the peak amplitude you set are the outer box, and the shape carries less charge than a rectangle of the same box (a half-sine carries 2/π ≈ 64 %, a linear ramp 50 %, and so on). PULSAR accounts for this automatically in the reported charge (see §7.4).

Asymmetric shape options

In Asymmetric biphasic mode an Asymmetric shape row appears with three choices:

  • Rectangular — both phases are flat-top; you set each amplitude and width independently.
  • Pseudo-capacitively-coupled — a rectangular cathodal phase paired with an exponential-decay anodal recharge, the profile a series capacitor produces Cogan 2008. The charge-balance solver derives the recharge automatically (see §7.4).
  • Mix and match — pick each phase's shape independently from its own dropdown (e.g. an exp-decay cathodal phase with a rectangular anodal phase). Charge balance still holds because the auto-balance arithmetic uses each phase's shape.
Restricted shapes & the custom catalog. A lab-specific build (for example the CWRU build) can add restricted shapes; those entries are hidden from the shape dropdowns until you log into the matching profile from the Admin menu (Log In…). The shapes listed above are the ones available in a standard PULSAR install. The Admin login additionally unlocks the custom catalog (Admin → Manage Custom Catalog); everyday testing never requires it.

7.4 Charge balance & auto-balance

A stimulation pulse should deliver net-zero charge per cycle so the electrode returns to its resting potential and no charge accumulates at the interface — the primary safeguard against irreversible electrochemistry and electrode/tissue damage Merrill 2005. The pattern panel keeps the pulse balanced for you:

  • Symmetric biphasic (and triphasic-ratio) patterns are balanced by construction — the reversal phase mirrors the excitation phase.
  • Asymmetric biphasic exposes a Charge-balance mode:
    • Auto-adjust last phase amplitude — recomputes the final phase's amplitude live so the net charge is zero.
    • Auto-adjust last phase width — does the same by adjusting the final phase's width.
    • Off (manual) — you set both phases freely; a warning appears if the pattern is not balanced.

Auto-balance works on the device grid (0.1 µA for an all-rectangular pattern, 30 nA if any phase is shaped), so the balance it computes is the balance the electrode actually receives.

The cap-coupled solve

The Pseudo-capacitively-coupled asymmetric shape has its own solver. Given the rectangular cathodal phase, it derives the exponential-decay anodal phase so the anodic charge magnitude exactly matches the cathodic:

  • Lock width — you pin the anodal width; the solver derives the peak amplitude and the decay time constant τ.
  • Lock amplitude — you pin the anodal peak; the solver derives the width and τ.
  • τ mode — Auto-derive ties τ to the geometry, or Manual τ lets you pin it (e.g. to match a measured electrode RC time constant, ~50–200 µs for a typical microelectrode).

If the ideal recharge would demand a peak above the stimulator's 1000 µA ceiling, the solver switches to a flat-top-then-decay shape (holds at 1000 µA, then decays) that still balances the charge. If the anodal window is too short for any 1000 µA recharge to deliver the required charge, the configuration is infeasible and the panel warns and refuses to load it rather than sending an unbalanced pulse.

7.5 Current offset (pedestal)

Non-rectangular shapes can ride on a baseline current offset — a floor the current never drops below, turning a ramp or a sine into a trapezoidal waveform that runs from the offset up to the peak instead of from zero. The Current offset checkbox (defaulted off) enables it; the offset field appears only for non-rectangular shapes, since a rectangle is already at its peak the whole time. Leave it off for standard pulses.

7.6 Interphase & discharge delays

Two zero-current gaps shape the timing of a pulse, each with its own checkbox and value:

  • Interphase delay — a gap between phases (e.g. between the cathodal and anodal phases). It lets the cathodic charge accumulate at the interface before the reversal phase, improving stimulation efficiency, and it makes the trailing access step and the anodic polarization cleanly measurable.
  • Discharge delay — a gap after the last phase, before the stimulator shorts the electrode to zero. This exposes the anodic (recovery) polarization on the recorded waveform so PULSAR can measure it.

Un-checking a delay's box forces that gap to 0 µs. These delays directly determine which access points and polarization values PULSAR can extract from the response — see the reading-the-plot section.

Auto-discharge. An Auto-discharge control (On by default) shorts the electrode between pulses to bleed off any residual charge. Turning it Off means any per-pulse charge imbalance accumulates and can drift the interface out of the safe water window — PULSAR shows a strong confirmation before allowing it. Leave auto-discharge On unless you specifically need the electrode to float between pulses.

7.7 Rate vs. frequency (continuous mode)

The pulse repeats at the rate you set. The rate control has a unit dropdown that toggles between pps (pulses per second) and a period in ms; the underlying rate is preserved when you switch units. The maximum rate is bounded both by the PlexStim ceiling (100,000 pps) and by the pulse width — one full pulse plus a 5 µs minimum interpulse gap must fit inside one period, so the ceiling drops as you widen the pulse.

The Interpulse delay checkbox does more than name the gap — it selects between two modes:

  • Checked (default) — there is a real gap after the discharge before the next pulse. The control is the Pulse rate in pps and you set it freely up to the width-limited ceiling.
  • Un-checked — the waveform is continuous (back-to-back pulses, no interpulse gap). The control becomes the Pulse frequency in Hz and stays editable in both directions:
    • edit the frequency and the phase widths rescale so the pulse fills exactly one period;
    • edit a width and the displayed frequency updates to match.
    Because the device's timing grid is 1 µs, a typed frequency snaps to the nearest achievable value on that grid.
Continuous symmetric sinusoids (KHFAC). A continuous symmetric biphasic sinusoid with no interphase, discharge, or interpulse delay is high-frequency alternating current. PULSAR detects this case and analyzes it with the Ghazavi access-resistance-corrected method rather than the pulsed edge metrics Ghazavi 2018 — see the reading-the-plot section.

7.8 Fixed charge-per-phase lock (Voltage Transient)

On the Voltage Transient parameters you can hold the charge per phase constant while you vary the pulse. Selecting the Fixed charge/phase mode exposes a three-way lock — current, width, or Qph — with a master lock checkbox (on by default). Whichever of the three you are not holding is recomputed live from Qph = I × W × d (with d the shape's duty factor), so the charge per phase stays fixed as you change current or width. Un-checking the lock frees current and width to be edited independently and shows the charge/phase as a read-only I×W display.

7.9 Live preview, Cadence view & acquisition time

The preview panel redraws the pulse as you edit. It shows both the ideal designed waveform and, where they differ, the device staircase — the sample-and-hold approximation the stimulator actually plays on its current grid — so you can see the quantization. A running summary reports the charge per phase (Qph), the net charge, the rate, and the total pulse width.

Which charge is reported? Every reported charge metric — Qph, Qinj, net charge, cumulative charge — uses the ideal continuous waveform (the true integral of the designed shape), so a 1000 µA × 200 µs linear ramp reads a clean 100.0 nC. The device staircase is used only inside the preview, to show the tiny quantization error versus that ideal — it never contaminates the numbers PULSAR saves.

Two aids sit alongside the preview:

  • Cadence button — the preview draws a continuous train of consecutive pulses; Cadence zooms the x-axis out to a few of them in one click, so you can see the pulse-to-pulse spacing (or, with no interpulse delay, the back-to-back run). Drag-pan or the X+/X− buttons then move along and fine-tune the scale.
  • Average count row — mirrors the oscilloscope's averaging count (the same setting as Setup → Oscilloscope acquisition → Average count; editing it here updates it everywhere). To its right an italic readout shows the approximate acquisition time per capture: in AVERAGE mode that is average count ÷ rate (each averaged sweep waits one pulse); in SAMPLE mode a single sweep. The readout mirrors your rate unit — it shows a division by pps, or a multiplication by the period in ms — so a 64-average capture at 100 pps reads ≈ 0.64 s / capture. It excludes trigger and transfer overhead, so it is a floor, not an exact timing.
Values are snapshotted at Start. PULSAR captures the whole pattern (and the Setup values) the moment you press Start. Edits made after that are ignored for the running experiment — change the pattern, then start a fresh run.

8 The experiments

PULSAR offers six experiment types, each with its own top‑level tab and its own parameter set on the Test parameters page. You pick the experiment from the experiment dropdown on the Setup tab; PULSAR then shows the matching experiment tab. All six share the same foundations — the authored pulse pattern (§6), the channel/combination selection grid, automatic scope scaling, the Start / Pause / Stop controls, and the same saved output files — so once you know one, the others are a short step.

The right experiment depends on what you want to learn: the largest current an electrode can inject safely (Voltage Transient), how its behaviour degrades under stepped stress (Progressive Stress), whether it stays stable over minutes to days (Short‑ / Continuous / Long‑Term Pulsing), or its impedance across frequency (Galvanostatic EIS).

8.1 Choosing an experiment

Experiment (abbr.)Current behaviourChannel / combo selectionHeadline result & when to use
Voltage Transient (VT) Adaptive upward ramp, per channel/combo, until the electrode polarization reaches the water‑window limit. Many — the whole array in one run (monopolar multi‑select; multipolar multi‑combo). Maximum charge‑injection capacity (max Qinj). The primary characterization run.
Progressive Stress (PS) Fixed‑charge staircase: steps the current up in fixed increments, holding each step. Several, tested sequentially (multipolar combos may not reuse a channel). How the metrics drift with stress. Use to stress‑test toward failure.
Short‑Term Pulsing (SP) Fixed amplitude for a set duration. One channel/combo. Quick “is this electrode stable?” check — a start‑vs‑end snapshot pair.
Continuous Pulsing (CP) Fixed amplitude, unbounded — pulses until you press Stop. One channel/combo. Open‑ended manual pulsing with periodic snapshots; you decide when to end.
Long‑Term Pulsing (LP) Fixed amplitude for hours‑to‑days, with periodic re‑characterization. Multiple monopolar channels (pulsed simultaneously); or one multipolar combo. Lifetime drift tracking. Resumable after a crash.
Galvanostatic Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) Small‑signal sinusoidal (or square) current, swept over frequency. No ramp. One channel/combo. Complex impedance Z(f) — a Bode and Nyquist plot.
Parameters are snapshotted at Start. Whatever is set on Setup and Test parameters when you press Start is what the run uses — edits made after Start are ignored for that run (a reminder is logged). To change something, Stop and Start again.

8.2 Voltage Transient (VT) — maximum charge‑injection capacity

VT is the canonical characterization run. For each selected channel/combo it sweeps the stimulus current upward and finds the largest current whose electrode polarization just reaches the water‑window limit — the maximum charge‑injection capacity, max Qinj (Nguyen et al.). Because a galvanostatic pulse that drives the interface past the water window causes irreversible electrolysis and electrode damage (Cogan 2008), the whole point of the ramp is to approach that boundary without crossing it.

How the ramp works

The sweep starts at the pattern's own amplitude — the first capture uses the pulse exactly as you drew it — and climbs from there. After each capture PULSAR fits the trend of polarization versus amplitude and predicts the current that will reach the limit, then steps toward it. The prediction is deliberately conservative (it undershoots), so the ramp lands just inside the water window rather than blowing past it. Three refinements keep it safe and fast:

  • Adaptive prediction. Far from the limit it takes large steps; as the polarization approaches the limit the steps shrink, so the crossover is resolved precisely without wasting captures.
  • Back‑off on overshoot. If a step lands the polarization past the acceptance band, PULSAR does not stop there — it brackets between the last safe amplitude and the overshoot and re‑captures at reduced amplitudes to settle the polarization back inside the band. The reported result is the true crossover, never an overshoot.
  • Early stop on a bad electrode. A capture classified open, broken, or capacitive has no Faradaic water window to ramp toward, so PULSAR stops that channel early instead of driving it to the hardware ceiling. (The 0 µA baseline capture of a “start at 0 µA” run is exempt — it carries no current to classify.)
Acceptance band. The limit is “reached” when the polarization lands within the small acceptance tolerance (§5.4, ≈20 mV) of the water‑window limit — a band centred on the limit, not a margin outside it. Because the ramp aims at the limit and the polarization curve flattens near it, the crossover is resolved to the fine testing resolution (0.1 µA).
Hardware‑limited result. If the ramp reaches the PlexStim ceiling (1000 µA/channel) without the polarization ever reaching the water window, the electrode's true ceiling is beyond what the stimulator can deliver: the last capture is flagged hardware‑limited and the reported max Qinj is a lower bound, not the achieved maximum.
VT is the “whole‑array” run. Select every channel (and every combo) you want characterized and press Start once — VT works through them in order, ticking each off as it completes, and writes them all into one session.

8.3 Progressive Stress (PS) — stepped‑current staircase

Progressive Stress drives one sample (a channel, or an active + return combo) through a staircase ramp: it holds a fixed current step for a set time, grabbing several averaged captures so metric drift within a step is recorded, then steps the current up and repeats. Unlike VT it does not predict a crossover — it is a “capture the voltage transient periodically at each current level” run, so you can track how access resistance, driving voltage, polarization, and charge evolve as the electrode is stressed.

The default staircase climbs from 5 µA in 5 µA steps, holding each step 60 s and capturing every 12 s. On the Test‑parameters page you set the step size, hold time, capture cadence, and the stop conditions. Each capture is tagged with its step level so the viewer can group them.

Stop conditions are explicit choices in the “Stop the ramp when…” group:

  • Maximum current (default on) — stop at a chosen ceiling; when off, the ramp runs to the PlexStim hardware limit (1000 µA), which is always the ultimate backstop.
  • Voltage compliance (default on) — stop when Vmon hits the stimulator's compliance rail (≈±9.6 V), beyond which the programmed current is no longer actually being delivered.
  • Manual stop — always available via the Stop button (shown for completeness; it cannot be turned off).
No automatic “failure” stop. PS deliberately does not auto‑stop on an electrochemical failure marker — the capacitive‑to‑Faradaic transition test from the DC‑encapsulation literature does not apply to AC stimulation electrodes and misfires here. PS records every metric over time; failure analysis is left to you (or POLARIS) after the run.

8.4 Short‑Term Pulsing (SP) — fixed amplitude, fixed duration

Short‑Term Pulsing is the simplest runner: it pulses the selected channel at a fixed amplitude for a set duration (default 60 s), taking full averaged snapshot captures so Vd, Va/Ra, Epol, and Qinj are computed for each. There is no ramp, no failure detection, and no re‑characterization — think of it as the manual / sanity‑check mode. For a typical short run PULSAR captures a snapshot at the start and takes one more at the end, giving you a start‑vs‑end pair to compare. SP runs the one selected channel/combo only.

8.5 Continuous Pulsing (CP) — pulse until you stop

Continuous Pulsing is Short‑Term Pulsing with an unbounded duration: it loads the pattern once, starts the stim, and pulses at a fixed amplitude until you press Stop, taking a snapshot capture on a cadence (default every 5 s). Pressing Stop is the designed way to end a continuous run, so the result is recorded as a normal completion, not an aborted run (a genuine error — e.g. a load failure — still marks the run aborted). Use it for open‑ended manual pulsing where you don't know the duration in advance.

8.6 Long‑Term Pulsing (LP) — drift tracking with re‑characterization

Long‑Term Pulsing pulses at a fixed safe amplitude for hours to days while periodically re‑measuring the full metric set, so you can watch Qinj, Vd, Ra, and polarization drift over the lifetime of the experiment. It interleaves two schedules on one continuous timeline:

  • Snapshots (default every 30 s) — a quick averaged capture with full metrics and a live waveform plot, so you always see the current electrode state.
  • Periodic feature — chosen from the Periodic feature dropdown: None, Maximum VT sweep (pause pulsing and run a short max‑Qinj characterization), Pause (stop pulsing for a set time so you can run an external instrument, e.g. a potentiostat), or Maximum VT sweep + Pause. When it is not None, you set the interval (in time or pulses) and can fire the first event at the start of the run. The paused time is excluded from the pulsing budget, so the fixed‑amplitude duration always means pulsing time.

Both schedules write into one time‑ordered session, so a “Qinj at t=0” and a “Qinj at t=12h” come from exactly the same code path.

Selection. For an all‑monopolar selection LP pulses every selected channel simultaneously (chronic array stimulation), cycling the scope monitor across them so each channel gets its own plot and metrics. A multipolar configuration is restricted to a single combo (conflicting return sets cannot be chronically co‑pulsed).

Resume after a crash. Press Resume from .npz… and pick a partially‑saved LP session; LP continues that run — appending new captures and picking up the snapshot cadence and remaining duration where the file left off — and saves back to the same file.

8.7 Galvanostatic EIS — impedance across frequency

Galvanostatic Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy applies a small‑signal sinusoidal (or square) current at a series of log‑spaced frequencies and, at each, computes the complex electrode impedance Z(f) = Vmon / Imon from a single‑bin lock‑in. There is no water‑window ramp — the probe amplitude is fixed and small (default 10 µA). The run's captures are the spectrum (one per frequency), from which the tab and POLARIS draw a Bode plot (|Z| and phase vs log f) and a Nyquist plot (−Z″ vs Z′).

On the Test‑parameters page you set the frequency range (default 1 Hz–100 kHz), points per decade, probe amplitude and shape, and an “Optimize for” mode (Fast / Normal / Low Noise) — modelled on Gamry's EIS setting, which trades speed against how many whole cycles are integrated per point. The maximum frequency is set by the 1 µs stimulator timing grid (about 125 kHz for a sine, up to 500 kHz for a square probe); a request above that is clamped and logged.

Why EIS needs no precise trigger. Z = V / I divides out any common time reference, so a free‑running frame spanning several whole cycles is enough — the multi‑cycle lock‑in is the averaging. EIS therefore runs in SAMPLE mode, unlike the averaged pulsed runs.

8.8 Channel & combination selection

Every experiment reads the sample(s) to test from the selection grid on the Test‑parameters page. A monopolar sample is a single active channel returning through the shared counter electrode; a multipolar sample (bipolar / tripolar / partial‑bipolar / partial‑tripolar) is an active channel plus a set of passive return channels — a combo. How many you can select depends on the experiment:

ExperimentMonopolarMultipolar (BP / TP / …)
Voltage TransientMulti‑select (whole array).Multi‑combo (the sweep loops over each).
Progressive StressMulti‑select, tested sequentially.Multiple combos, but no channel may be reused across selected combos (they run sequentially and a channel cannot be both active and return, or shared, twice).
Long‑Term PulsingMulti‑select — pulsed simultaneously.Single combo only.
Short‑Term / Continuous Pulsing, EISOne channel/combo per run.

Monopolar is always multi‑select so you can characterize a whole array in one run. The multipolar restrictions reflect the physics: LP cannot chronically co‑pulse combos with conflicting return sets, and PS steps disjoint combos in turn so no channel is stressed twice.

8.9 Stop conditions & safety limits

A run ends for one of these reasons (which apply depends on the experiment):

ConditionWhat it meansApplies to
Water‑window limit The electrode polarization (Emc / Ema) reached the cathodic / anodic limit set on Setup (e.g. −0.6 V / +0.8 V for SIROF) — the safe charge‑injection ceiling (Cogan 2008). VT stops the ramp here. VT
Hardware ceiling The current reached the PlexStim maximum (1000 µA/channel). A VT that reaches this without hitting the water window reports a lower‑bound max Qinj (hardware‑limited). VT, PS
Voltage compliance Vmon hit the stimulator's compliance rail (≈±9.6 V); beyond it the device is no longer delivering the programmed current. Filtered over 3 consecutive samples so a noise spike can't trip it. VT, PS (selectable)
Bad response A capture classified open, broken, or capacitive has no water window to ramp toward — VT stops that channel early rather than driving it to the ceiling. VT
Blind‑ramp safety stop For a continuous (KHFAC) sinusoid, if the polarization stays unmeasurable as the current climbs, the ramp refuses to drive blind and stops (a washed capture or a broken electrode) — continuous stimulation gives no interpulse rest, so it is ramped extra‑gently. VT (continuous patterns)
Duration reached The configured pulsing time elapsed (paused time excluded). SP, LP
Manual Stop You pressed Stop. The run ends as soon as it is safely possible. For Continuous Pulsing this is the normal end of the run. All
The water‑window limits are yours to set correctly. PULSAR will not knowingly ramp past the cathodic / anodic limits configured on the Setup tab, but those values are only as safe as the electrode material and reference you entered. Confirm them before a VT run — they are the electrochemical safety boundary (Merrill et al. 2005).

9 Running an experiment

Once the hardware is connected and the pattern is authored, a run is driven from the three run controls at the bottom of every experiment page — Start, Pause / Continue, and Stop. This section walks through what happens between pressing Start and the files landing on disk, and how the controls behave.

9.1  The three‑step lead‑up

  1. On Setup, connect the stimulator and oscilloscope, choose the device/array and coating/area, map the scope channels, set the acquisition mode, trigger, and water‑window limits, and pick the save folder.
  2. On Test parameters, author the pulse pattern, select the channel(s)/combo(s) in the selection grid, and set the parameters for the chosen experiment (ramp strategy, duration, stop conditions, and so on).
  3. Press Start.

9.2  What Start snapshots

Pressing Start takes a one‑time snapshot of every Setup and Test‑parameters value the run needs — active channel and returns, the pulse pattern, ramp policy, surface area, water‑window limits, scope mapping, and cable translation. PULSAR logs a one‑liner confirming this. Edits you make after Start are ignored for that run; they take effect on the next Start press.

Why a snapshot. A characterization run reads its parameters once so the sweep is reproducible and self‑documenting — the numbers saved with the data are exactly the ones that were in effect. If you meant to change something, Stop, change it, and Start again.

The device→Plexon cable translation is also logged at Start, so you can confirm that a pulse you requested on device channel N actually commands the intended Plexon stimulator channel (identity for the test board and standard cables; a remap for others).

9.3  The two Start‑time safety prompts

Before touching any hardware, Start runs two quick checks. Either can be cancelled cleanly — cancelling leaves all your inputs exactly as they were.

SituationPrompt
The save folder does not exist yet (e.g. a mistyped path).Create the folder and continue, or Cancel to go back and fix the save location. This catches an accidental path before the run silently creates a stray folder.
Starting would replace existing files (a previous run used the same folder + filename).The dialog lists the files that would be overwritten and offers Continue (overwrite), Append to filename (saves as <stem>_2, _3, … alongside the existing data), or Cancel. The session log (.txt) is included as an overwrite candidate too.
I‑mon trigger needs current. If the trigger source is the Imon current edge (typical on a 2‑channel scope with no digital sync), the first phase's amplitude must be at least |0.1 µA| — below that the current is too small to trigger reliably. Start is blocked with a message; raise the amplitude, or add a digital Trigger channel (needed for a Voltage‑Transient ramp that starts at 0 µA).
Re‑initializing the stimulator. If the previous run was Stopped (which closes the stimulator, see §9.6), or the device otherwise reports closed, Start automatically re‑initializes it first. Back‑to‑back normal runs skip this — the stimulator stays open between them.

9.4  Configuring the scope (the 10‑30 s wait)

After the prompts, PULSAR configures the oscilloscope for the run: it enables the mapped channels (with the resolved coupling and bandwidth), sets the record length (20 000 points by default), the acquisition mode and average count, the trigger, the horizontal timebase framed to your pulse, and an initial vertical scale for each channel. A status‑bar message reads “Configuring scope (this can take 10‑30 s on TBS2000 with large records)…”.

Why it can take up to half a minute. On a TBS2000‑series scope, changing the record length triggers an internal capture‑buffer reallocation that can take 10‑30 seconds. PULSAR pumps the interface during this window so the window stays responsive and the log pane fills in real time — it is not frozen. The experiment view appears, and pulsing begins, once configuration completes.
Scope auto‑scaling. During the run PULSAR sizes each channel's vertical scale and position on every capture so the waveform fills the screen without clipping (the fit‑the‑view rescale step in the diagram). You never need to touch the scope's front panel during a run.

9.5  What happens during the run

The runner loops over amplitudes/steps as shown in the diagram. For each step it loads the pattern on the active channel (and a zero‑amplitude copy on unused channels so they tick in cadence but deliver no current), pulses, takes an averaged capture, rescales the view, and extracts the metrics. The live plot and the metrics table update as each capture completes; the log pane records every step. Each capture is also written to disk incrementally, so data collected so far survives a crash or disconnect.

The parameter inputs (pattern panel, experiment parameters, channel grid) are locked for the duration of the run, but you can still scroll and read them, and you can freely switch between the Setup, Test parameters, and experiment tabs while it runs.

9.6  The progress bar

A thin progress bar with a label sits above the plot. What it shows depends on the experiment, because some runs have a fixed duration and others (the adaptive ramps) do not:

ExperimentProgress display
Short / Long Pulsing (fixed duration)A fractional time bar — elapsed / total seconds and (pulses delivered / total pulses).
Continuous Pulsing (unbounded)A busy (marquee) bar with running elapsed‑time and pulse counts — there is no total to divide by.
Voltage Transient (adaptive ramp)A channel‑step bar — channels/combos completed of the total selected — because the amplitude ramp has no known length.
Progressive StressNo dedicated bar; per‑channel progress is shown in the status bar.

9.7  Pause / Continue and Stop

Pause / Continue

Press Pause to halt pulsing and hold — the button relabels to Continue. Pressing Continue resumes the run where it left off: the stimulator's loaded patterns are retained across the pause, so resuming simply restarts them. For a time‑bounded run (Short/Long Pulsing), the paused interval is excluded from the run duration, so a pause doesn't shorten the pulsing you asked for. Pressing Stop while paused aborts immediately.

Stop

Stop ends the run as soon as it is safely possible. It immediately aborts any pulse in flight (a DLL‑safe abort, valid in any trigger mode) and requests the runner to unwind; a blocking scope read in progress bails out promptly rather than waiting out its full timeout. Captures already taken are saved.

Stop tears the stimulator down; Start rebuilds it. On Stop, PULSAR aborts the stimulator and — once the run's worker thread has fully exited — closes it, leaving the device in a fully clean state.
