The next Start press re‑initializes it automatically (§9.3). This deliberate close‑then‑reinit cycle avoids a hardware race that could otherwise corrupt the stimulator DLL, so do use Stop rather than yanking the USB cable.

9.8  Camera capture during a run

If a camera is connected and you enabled the Camera capture during run options on the Test‑parameters page, Start arms them: an optional periodic snapshot (default every 30 s, minimum 1 s) and/or a single MP4 recording that runs for the whole experiment. Both are torn down on every exit path — normal end, abort, or error. With the toggles on but no camera connected, PULSAR logs a note and simply skips them.

9.9  When the run ends

On normal completion PULSAR logs the total elapsed time, shows a small “Experiment finished in …” pop‑up, marks each completed channel/combo with a ✓ in the entry list, and re‑enables the inputs. The final data — the capture .npz, the metric workbook .xlsx, and the per‑channel figures — is saved to your chosen folder (file stem = notebook + session).

Aborted runs are flagged in the filenames. If a run is Stopped or aborts, its session‑level files are renamed with an _ABORTED suffix (e.g. notebook_subject_ABORTED.npz) and the .npz is marked incomplete internally, so partial data is unmistakable in the file browser and in POLARIS. Per‑channel figures already written keep their names — a channel figure is valid data regardless.
Everything is re‑openable. The plot, markers, and every metric you saw during the run are stored in the files above and can be re‑examined, re‑classified, and re‑exported in POLARIS at any time (see §12).

10 Reading the plot & metrics

Every experiment tab shows the same two panels side by side: a live scope plot of the recorded traces with metric markers overlaid, and a metrics table listing the numeric values for the capture currently shown in the plot. The plot and the table are always locked to the same capture — if you scroll back through earlier captures with the per‑capture dropdown, or pin a completed channel while a later one streams in, the table follows the waveform on screen. This section explains how to read both, what each marker means, and how the headline numbers are defined.

The plot is white on purpose. The waveform plots always render on a white background with black axes, matching the exported figures — the View → Theme light/dark setting styles only the surrounding window chrome, not the plots.

10.1 The traces

Up to four recorded channels are drawn, colour‑coded by role. Voltages share the left axis; the current shares a separate right axis whose zero is aligned with the voltage zero.

TraceColourAxisWhat it is
VmonGolden yellowLeft The voltage monitor — the voltage across the electrode (active vs return). Always present.
ImonTealRight The current monitor — the delivered stimulus current.
EactBluish‑greenLeft Active‑electrode potential vs the reference electrode, when an instrumentation amplifier is digitized. If only Eret is recorded, Eact is derived as Vmon + Eret and labelled (calculated).
EretVermillionLeft Return‑electrode potential vs the reference electrode, when recorded.

The trace colours are identical on the live plot, in POLARIS, and in the saved figures, so a screenshot and a .tif read the same. Individual traces can be toggled on and off from the column of checkboxes to the left of the plot (for a multi‑capture overlay) or by clicking a legend entry.

10.2 Axis labels & units

Reference‑aware voltage label

PULSAR names the left (voltage) axis automatically by what is on it:

  • Only electrode potentials (Eact / Eret, no raw Vmon) → Potential vs <reference> [V] (the reference electrode name, defaulting to Ag|AgCl) — because these are measured against the reference.
  • Only Vmon (no potentials) → Voltage vs <return> [V] (the return / counter electrode, defaulting to Pt) — because Vmon is the active‑vs‑return driving voltage.
  • A mix of both → the plain Voltage [V].

This relabelling is fully automatic (there are no checkboxes for it) and is suppressed for the Plexon Test Board, which has no electrodes — that device always shows the plain Voltage [V].

Current vs current density

A small unit dropdown next to the Imon axis switches the right axis between µA (the default) and A/cm² (current density). The density option appears only when a non‑zero electrode surface area is set on the Setup tab; clearing the area snaps the axis back to µA.

10.3 The inset & derivative overlays

  • Inset — a single‑select trace picker parks one trace in a small inset beside the main plot, with its own axes. The inset trace need not also be visible in the main plot, and it picks up the same reference‑aware voltage label. An Imon inset shows µA or A/cm² per the unit dropdown (a single current axis — no separate density scale).
  • dV/dt and 1/(dV/dt) — optional analysis overlays (Harris 2019). They are drawn as normalized, dashed curves on the voltage axis (shape only — their true V/µs and reciprocal scales don't fit the axis), and are off by default; enable them from the per‑trace axis controls.
  • E′act / E′ret — for a continuous‑sinusoid (KHFAC) capture only, PULSAR also draws dashed access‑resistance‑corrected interface potentials (the measured trace minus the ohmic drop Raccess·I), after Ghazavi 2018. See §10.7.

10.4 The metric markers

PULSAR overlays the extracted electrochemical quantities directly on the waveform. Every marker is placed on a despiked copy of the trace — a ~4 µs median filter that rejects the sharp switching spikes and ringing at each phase boundary, so a transient can never be mistaken for the driving peak or an access plateau. Markers are drawn on the active‑electrode trace (Eact, recorded or derived) when it is available, otherwise on Vmon.

MarkerGlyph · colourWhere & what
Va / Ra
access voltage / resistance		 Horizontal bar · crimson The instantaneous ohmic (IR) step at each current edge, read on the post‑step plateau. One marker at every access point — leading and trailing — so the count depends on the pattern: an interphase delay adds trailing‑phase‑1 and leading‑phase‑2 points, a discharge delay adds a trailing point on the last phase. The tag shows Va and, on a second line, Ra = Va / I (Cogan 2008).
Vd
driving voltage		 + · cobalt One marker at the peak excursion of the driving phase (the phase with the largest |amplitude|; ties resolve to phase 1, so a symmetric biphasic uses phase 1). Its value is the Vmon change from the pre‑pulse baseline — the compliance the stimulator must supply. A phase that is preceded by an interphase delay gets its own additional Vd2 marker, referenced to the recovered end‑of‑interphase voltage.
Emc / Ema
electrode polarization		 + · violet The maximum cathodic (Emc) and anodic (Ema) interface polarization, with the IR drop removed. A cathodal phase is labelled Emc, an anodal phase Ema (a numeric suffix is added only when the same polarity repeats, e.g. a triphasic pulse). These are compared against the water‑window limits — see §10.6.
Response annotation x · black On a bad electrode (open / broken / capacitive) PULSAR draws a single black x with the response class and the relevant fit (see §10.8) instead of the access / driving / polarization markers.
The marker value equals the table value. The Emc/Ema figure on the plot is read from the very same per‑phase polarization the table shows and the water‑window check uses (§10.6) — the plot, the table, and the ramp‑stop decision can never disagree. Labels are placed by a scoring routine that keeps each tag off the traces (both axes), off the screen edges, and clear of the other labels; there are no leader lines.

Thin dashed vertical guide lines also mark each phase's expected polarization location (the phase end plus 12 µs, for phases that have a trailing recovery delay). These are a geometric reference from the programmed timing — useful for eyeballing whether the measured Emc/Ema landed where the pattern says it should, especially for smooth sinusoidal or gaussian shapes. At a 0 µA baseline capture no markers or guides are drawn (there is no current, so nothing to measure).

10.5 The metrics table

For a normal capture the table lists, top to bottom:

RowMeaning
NpulseNumber of pulses delivered to acquire this capture (the measured pulsing time × the pulse rate). Falls back to a capture index for the continuous‑pulsing experiments.
Istim [µA]The excitation‑phase amplitude of the pulse delivered for this capture.
Qph [nC]Charge per phase — the ideal time‑integral of the current over the excitation phase.
Qinj [mC/cm²]Charge‑injection density — Qph normalized by electrode area.
Pulse rate [pps] · Pulse periodThe pattern's repetition rate and its period.
Cumulative Npulse · Cumulative QPulses and cathodic charge delivered so far in the run, building on earlier captures (auto‑scaled nC / µC / mC). Shown for the discrete‑burst experiments (VT, PS).
Eip [V]Interpulse (rest) potential — omitted when the pattern has no interpulse gap to measure it in.
Cd [mF/cm²]Driving capacitance — max Qinj / Vd (a charge/voltage efficiency ratio, not a double‑layer capacitance).
Zd [kΩ] · Driving energyDriving impedance (Vd / Istim) and the pulse energy (∫ Vmon·I dt using the ideal programmed current), when finite.
Cdl · Faradaic fraction · Faradaic onsetChronopotentiometric double‑layer capacitance and the approximate capacitive/Faradaic charge split (Harris 2019) — shown only for a functional rectangular pulse with a known area.
Vd [V]The per‑phase driving voltage(s). With a separate Eact/Eret recorded, the table splits this into Vd active and Vd return; without one, Vmon is the active‑vs‑return voltage, so a single unqualified Vd is shown.
Va / Ra [V] / [kΩ]Access voltage and resistance at each access point (plus return‑side rows when instrumented, and a Va (peak I) row for smooth shaped phases that have no current edge).
Epol [V]The per‑phase electrode polarization (active, and return when recorded) — the same values as the Emc/Ema markers.
Limit reached? · Limit exceeded? · Compliance exceeded?Whether the polarization entered the water‑window band, overshot past its far edge, or the stimulator hit its voltage compliance (see §10.6).

Multi‑value per‑phase rows are comma‑separated and word‑wrap so every value is visible.

10.6 Electrode polarization & the water‑window band

Epol is the interface polarization with the ohmic access drop removed — the quantity that must stay inside the electrode's safe potential (water) window. PULSAR uses the lab's operator method to place it per phase:

  • A phase with a trailing recovery delay (interphase or discharge) → the potential 12 µs after the phase end, sampled in the quiet window once the current has settled to zero (the IEEE NER Emc convention, Cogan 2008).
  • A delay‑less phase boundary → driving potential − leading access voltage for that phase (there is no quiet window to sample, so the IR drop is subtracted arithmetically).
  • A phase that is neither (e.g. the second phase of a delay‑less biphasic with no discharge delay) → undetermined — no value, and no marker is drawn.
The acceptance band. The cathodic and anodic limits you set on the Setup tab are the centre of an acceptance band whose half‑width is the tolerance (default 0.020 V). The limit counts as reached when Epol lands within ±tolerance of it — a rising ramp enters the band at the near edge (limit + tolerance), so the Voltage‑Transient sweep stops there rather than creeping past. A step that overshoots past the band's far edge is flagged separately as Limit exceeded?. This band is exactly what makes the adaptive VT ramp find the maximum safe charge injection without driving the electrode past the water window (Merrill 2005).
You own the limit values. The water‑window limits are the electrochemical safety boundary for your electrode material and reference. PULSAR will not knowingly ramp past them, but it uses the numbers you enter — set them correctly for your electrode.

10.7 KHFAC & EIS variants

Two experiment modes produce non‑standard captures with their own metrics.

Continuous sinusoid (KHFAC)

A continuous symmetric sinusoid has no current‑step edge, so the pulsed access/polarization method does not apply. PULSAR instead uses the Ghazavi 2018 decomposition, splitting the measured voltage into a resistive part (in phase with the current, the access) and the interface potential. The metrics table then shows the phase‑decomposition set instead of the pulsed rows:

  • Emc / Ema — max cathodic / anodic interface excursion (compared to the water window, exactly as for pulses).
  • Eio / Eoff — interface swing amplitude and DC offset.
  • Vaccess / Raccess — the resistive access voltage and resistance.
  • Phase angle φ of each voltage trace vs Imon (≈ 0° resistive, → −90° capacitive), with Imon shown as the 0° reference.
  • Pulse frequency [kHz] in place of the pulse‑rate row.

These are reported for the active electrode, and for the return electrode when Eret is recorded. The dashed E′act/E′ret interface traces (§10.3) are the graphical form of this correction.

Galvanostatic EIS

The Galvanostatic EIS experiment sweeps a small sinusoidal current over frequency and computes the complex impedance at each point (|Z|, phase, and the real / imaginary parts). Its results are presented on dedicated Bode and Nyquist sub‑plots rather than in the per‑capture metrics table; there is no water‑window ramp.

10.8 Bad‑response captures

PULSAR classifies each capture's electrode response and, for a bad electrode, replaces the normal markers and rows with a focused diagnosis (the Voltage‑Transient ramp also stops early on one).

ClassWhat it means & what is shown
normalA functional electrode — the full access / driving / polarization markers and metrics above.
openDisconnected / very high impedance with no ohmic access step. The plot shows the black x annotation; the table shows the response and an effective capacitance Ceff. Access / Epol are suppressed.
brokenA degraded electrode fitted to a parallel R‖C model — the table shows the fitted R, C, and time constant τ (per phase where available).
capacitiveA purely capacitive response (a clean linear ramp with no resolvable access step) — reported with Ceff.
Why capacitance is only shown for bad captures. A pulse‑derived effective capacitance is not a defensible number for a functional electrode, where resistive, capacitive, and Faradaic contributions cannot be cleanly separated (Harris 2024). PULSAR therefore reports Ceff only for the open / capacitive / broken cases, where the response really is dominated by a single mechanism, and reports voltages and charge — not capacitance — for a normal electrode.
All the same numbers, later. Every trace, marker, and table value on this plot is saved with the capture. You can re‑open, re‑examine, edit the response class, and re‑export any of it in POLARIS at any time, with no hardware attached (see the POLARIS section).

11 Stimulator verification

Verification (optional) checks the stimulator's delivered current and its Vmon / Imon monitor scaling against a known test board, over a sweep of amplitudes. It fits the load R and C and the per‑channel monitor gain. Verification is not required to run experiments — the stimulator's scaling preset is detected automatically at Initialize. Run it if you want to confirm the monitors, or after changing hardware.

12 Output files

WhatWhere
Per‑run capture data (.npz), metric workbook (.xlsx), per‑channel figures (.tif/.png/.svg), session log (.txt)Your chosen save folder (file stem = notebook + session).
Preferences, stimulator calibration, learned electrode potentials%APPDATA%\StimulationTesting\ (survives uninstall)
Crash / launch error logsThe project tree (next to your session files), never %TEMP%.

An aborted run marks its files with an _ABORTED suffix so incomplete data is obvious.

13 POLARIS session viewer

POLARIS opens and reviews saved data with no hardware attached. Launch it from the Start Menu (or open a .npz file with it).

12.1  Opening data

  • Open… a single session (.npz), or Open folder… to index a directory of sessions. Files accumulate in the tree; use Remove (or the Delete key) to drop one from view.
  • Import external scope captures — PicoScope exports in .csv, .tsv, or .xls/.xlsx. Assign channel roles (and a current scale) to compute metrics from them.

12.2  Navigating

Expand a session in the left tree to reach its runs and individual captures. Selecting a node shows its plot and three tables: Metric (waveform metrics), Parameters (experiment settings), and File info.

12.3  Viewing & overlays

  • Select a channel/combo to overlay all its captures; toggle individual traces on/off from the column of checkboxes or by clicking legend entries.
  • Plot controls — override X / left‑Y / right‑Y axis ranges, switch the current axis between µA and current density, add dV/dt / 1/(dV/dt) overlays, or open the charge‑transfer (dE/dt) analysis view.
  • Styles… — set per‑trace color and line style; changes persist across captures.

12.4  Editing metrics

You can override a channel/combo's response class (Good / Broken / Open / Capacitive) — the appropriate metrics are recomputed — and hand‑edit selected metric values, then Save to file to write the changes back to the .npz (the raw waveforms are preserved).

12.5  Exporting

PULSAR already auto‑exports per‑channel figures and a metric workbook. In POLARIS you can re‑render any capture's figure and, via the Gamry‑DTA‑style workbook, review the per‑capture summary and raw data table.

14 Troubleshooting

SymptomFix
“No Plexon Stimulator is detected”Close Plexon Stim‑2 (it holds the USB lock), then press Initialize. Only one program can own the stimulator.
Initialize hangs / window “Not Responding”The stimulator init runs on a background thread and shows a hint after ~15 s. Close Stim‑2 and/or power‑cycle the stimulator, then retry.
Scope “semaphore timeout” on ConnectLeftover USB claim from a prior crash — PULSAR auto‑retries; if it persists, power‑cycle the scope and replug USB.
“Access is denied” when savingUsually a transient OneDrive sync lock — retry the save, or point the Save location at a non‑OneDrive folder (e.g. C:\PULSAR_data) to avoid it.
Current reads absurd values / monitors look wrongRe‑run Verification with a clean signal (or reset the calibration); PULSAR ignores an implausible saved monitor gain on load.
A channel is flagged Open/Broken and the VT ramp stops earlyThat electrode's response has no measurable access resistance (open) or is degraded (broken). Check the connection; the classification is amplitude‑independent.
SmartScreen / antivirus blocks the installerClick More info → Run anyway, or give IT the SHA‑256 in the whitelist note included with this download.

If PULSAR fails to launch, a diagnostic is written to pulsar_launch_error.log in the project tree (or next to your session files). Include it when reporting a problem.

15 Glossary of metrics

This glossary defines every metric PULSAR reports, using the exact abbreviation shown in the app. Units are carried in each metric‑table row label in square brackets (e.g. Istim [µA], Qph [nC], Qinj [mC/cm2]). The per‑capture metric table (and the POLARIS viewer) has three view modes, each showing a different subset: a normal functional‑electrode view, a focused bad‑response view (open / broken / capacitive), and a KHFAC view for continuous symmetric‑sinusoidal (kilohertz‑frequency AC) captures.

Epol versus Emc / Ema. The metric table abbreviates the general per‑phase electrode polarization as Epol (rows “Epol active” / “Epol return”). Emc (maximum cathodic excursion) and Ema (maximum anodic excursion) are the polarity‑labelled entries of that same per‑phase series — they appear as the plot markers (a cathodal phase → Emc, an anodal phase → Ema) and as KHFAC table rows. The marker value is read straight from the stored per‑phase polarization, so the plot and the table can never disagree.

Where an active/return instrumentation amplifier (Eact / Eret) is recorded, per‑phase voltages split into “active” and “return” rows; without one, Vmon is the active‑vs‑return voltage, the “active” qualifier is dropped, and the per‑phase values are shown as a single comma‑joined list.

TermDefinition
Stimulus & charge
Stimulus current amplitude (Istim) [µA] The programmed excitation‑phase current amplitude of the pulse — the driving stimulus current. Read directly from the pattern (not derived from the scope trace). Shown in the normal, bad‑response and KHFAC views.
Stimulus current density (Jstim) [A/cm2] Stimulus current per geometric electrode area (Istim ÷ area). Shown in the per‑channel plot heading / exported‑figure subtitle when a surface area is configured; omitted for the Plexon Test Board (no area). Not a metric‑table row.
Charge per phase (Qph) [nC] Charge injected in the excitation phase — the ideal continuous (trapezoidal) integral of the programmed, as‑designed current waveform over the phase, computed on the unquantized breakpoints (not the device staircase). Shown in the normal, bad‑response and KHFAC views and in the exported SUMMARY.
Charge‑injection density (Qinj) [mC/cm2] Injected charge per unit geometric electrode area for the excitation phase = (Qph in nC) ÷ area. NaN when no area is set. In plot headings it auto‑rescales to µC/cm2 when it would round to 0.000 mC/cm2. Shown in the normal and KHFAC views and the plot heading.
Maximum charge‑injection capacity (max Qinj) [mC/cm2] The headline VT result — the largest Qinj achieved across a run’s captures before the water‑window potential limit (or the hardware‑current ceiling) stopped the ramp. Computed over captures that are good and did not overshoot the limit (over‑window captures are excluded). Shown in the POLARIS run/channel summary.
Voltages & potentials
Driving voltage (Vd) [V] The voltage the stimulator must drive to deliver the pulse, per phase = |reference − trace| sampled ~1 µs before the phase ends (the settled peak excursion, off the trailing access drop); the reference is the pre‑pulse baseline (phase 1) or the end‑of‑prior‑interphase level (later phases). It is the active‑vs‑return driving potential (Vmon). Shown as a comma‑joined per‑phase list (splitting into Vd active / Vd return with an instrumentation amp); the legacy scalar is max|Vmon|. Drawn on the plot as the Vd (and Vd2, Vd3…) markers.
Access voltage (Va) [V] The instantaneous ohmic (IR) voltage step at each current edge — the pure IR jump when the current steps to or from zero, with the capacitive cap‑ramp and source rise‑time subtracted out (pre‑edge and post‑edge linear fits extrapolated to the |dV/dt| edge peak). One entry per access point — leading and trailing of each phase, so the count depends on the pattern (an interphase delay adds a trailing‑phase‑1 and leading‑phase‑2 point; a discharge delay adds a trailing point). Numbered Va1…VaN on the plot; active side on Eact, return side on Eret when recorded.
Access resistance (Ra) [kΩ] The electrolyte + spreading (series/access) resistance at each current edge = Va ÷ I for that phase. Reported per access point (active and return); shown as the second line of each Va plot marker (Cogan 2008).
Peak‑current access (Va (peak I) / Ra (peak I)) [V] / [kΩ] For smooth shaped phases (gaussian / sinusoidal) that have no current‑step edge, the access voltage and resistance measured at peak current instead: Ra = least‑squares slope of V vs I over the phase, Va = |Ra|·|Ipeak|. A separate measurement — it does not feed the Epol / water‑window decision. Excludes rectangular, pedestal‑offset and KHFAC phases.
Interphase / interpulse potential (Eip) [V] The settled inter‑pulse rest (open‑circuit) potential of the return/reference electrode — the mean of the Eret trace outside the active pulse (pre‑pulse baseline plus post‑discharge tail). Returns NaN when the pattern has no idle interpulse gap (the period is fully occupied, so there is no true rest window). Shown in the normal view and the SUMMARY.
Electrode polarization & water window
Electrode polarization (Epol) [V] The per‑phase electrode polarization — the interface potential excursion driven by the phase, referenced past the ohmic access drop (the “operator” method: a time sample at phase end + depolarization for phases with a trailing delay, else |driving − leading access|; NaN when undetermined). Measured on Eact when recorded, else Vmon. This is the value the metric table shows and the water‑window limit trip uses; the plot’s Emc/Ema markers read the same series. Shown per phase (active and return) in the normal view.
Maximum cathodic / anodic excursion (Emc / Ema) [V] The maximum cathodic excursion (Emc, most‑negative interface potential) and maximum anodic excursion (Ema, most‑positive), compared against the water‑window limits. For pulsed patterns these are the cathodic/anodic entries of the per‑phase Epol series (labelled by phase polarity, with a suffix like Emc1/Emc2 only when a polarity repeats); for KHFAC they are the min/max of the de‑ohm’d interface potential (Ghazavi). Drawn with the “+” plot glyph.
Water window The potential range within which the electrode charges reversibly without irreversible electrolysis (the cathodic / anodic potential limits, vs the reference electrode). The safety boundary the VT‑max ramp targets; the ramp stops when Epol lands within an acceptance band centered on the limit.
Limit reached? · Limit exceeded? [boolean] Limit reached = the polarization landed within ±tolerance of the water‑window limit (a clean stop). Limit exceeded = it overshot past the band’s far edge (an over‑window overshoot, excluded from max Qinj). Shown in every view.
Compliance exceeded? [boolean] Whether the stimulator hit its ±9 V voltage‑compliance limit delivering the programmed current (electrode/circuit impedance too high for the current source; multi‑sample check on Vmon). Shown in every view.
Capacitance, impedance & energy
Driving (charge‑storage) capacitance (Cd) [mF/cm2] A charge‑per‑volt efficiency ratio (not a double‑layer capacitance): max Qinj (mC/cm2) ÷ Vd (V) = mF/cm2 — the injected charge density delivered per volt across the whole active‑return driving circuit. Shown in the normal view and the SUMMARY.
Driving impedance (Zd) [kΩ] The total impedance the stimulator drives into during the driving phase (access resistance + polarization) = |Vd| ÷ |Istim|. Shown in the normal view (when finite) and the SUMMARY.
Driving energy [µJ, auto‑scaled pJ/nJ/µJ/mJ] The electrical energy delivered to the electrode per pulse = ∫ Vmon·I dt integrated over the whole pulse (all phase windows; passive gaps carry ~0 current). Uses the ideal programmed current, not the measured Imon (which carries switching spikes and turn‑on skew). Shown in the normal view (when finite) and as SUMMARY column “Energy”.
Double‑layer capacitance (Cdl) [mF/cm2] The electrode double‑layer capacitance from the constant‑dE/dt (purely capacitive) window of the driving phase (Harris 2019 chronopotentiometry): Cdl = I / (A·dE/dt). Amplitude‑independent — the defensible areal capacitance. Shown in the normal view only, and only for a rectangular (constant‑current) pulse on a functional electrode with a known area.
Faradaic charge fraction [%] An approximate, first‑order estimate of the fraction of phase charge carried by Faradaic (redox) rather than capacitive current: Qfaradaic / Qtotal, with Qcap = A·Cdl·ΔEpol. A galvanostatic pulse cannot cleanly separate the two, so treat this as indicative. Shown in the normal view when finite.
Faradaic onset [µs (with V)] The time (and potential) at which dE/dt first sustainedly dips below the capacitive baseline — where Faradaic reactions begin diverting current. NaN for a ~purely capacitive phase (no resolvable onset). Shown in the normal view when finite.
Effective capacitance (Ceff) [nF] Effective capacitance Ceff = |I| / |dV/dt| from the linear charging‑ramp slope. Reported only for a degenerate capacitive or open response, where there is no separable resistive + Faradaic component so I/(dV/dt) is meaningful. NaN (and omitted) for a normal mixed electrode, whose access / Epol values are reported instead.
R∥C fit capacitance (C) [nF] For a broken (exponential) response, the capacitance from a parallel‑R∥C fit V = V∞(1−e−t/τ), C = τ/R. Labelled a bare C (not Ceff). Shown in the bad‑response view, per phase.
R∥C fit resistance (R (R∥C)) [kΩ] For a broken electrode, the leakage/Faradaic resistance from the parallel‑R∥C exponential fit, R = V∞/I. Shown in the bad‑response view, per phase.
R∥C fit time constant (τ (R∥C)) [µs] The time constant τ = RC of the broken‑electrode parallel‑R∥C exponential fit. Shown in the bad‑response view, per phase.
Response classification & electrode health
Response class (Response) The electrode response category that decides which conditional metrics are reported: normal (functional resistive + capacitive + Faradaic → access Va/Ra + Epol), capacitive or open (a straight charging ramp, disconnected / high‑impedance, no access step → Ceff only), or broken (an exponential response → R∥C fit R, C, τ). Shown UPPERCASE in the bad‑response view; a normal capture omits the row.
Access‑resistance drift (Ra drift: p / flag) A per‑run electrode‑health test: a two‑sided Mann–Whitney U comparison of the recent Ra window against the run’s earlier Ra (0 µA captures excluded). Flags when the p‑value is significant and the median shift is physically meaningful — a signature of a degrading / broken electrode. Warn‑only (an edge‑triggered log line; never stops the run).
Shannon k‑value & tissue‑damage screen (Shannon k) A tissue‑damage safety index, k = log10(charge density) + log10(charge per phase), with k ≈ 1.5–2 the conventional damage threshold (Shannon 1992). Computed from Qph and Qinj along with a damage classification (likely‑safe / above‑Shannon / above macro‑ or micro‑electrode caps) and an optional NeurostimML second opinion. Guidance only — Shannon misclassifies a substantial fraction of damaging stimulation as safe. Surfaced in POLARIS and the pre‑run damage warning.
Counts, cumulative dose & timing
Number of pulses (Npulse) [count] The number of stimulation pulses delivered to acquire this capture = pulsing duration × pulse rate (for an averaged acquisition, the averaging count). First row of every view; set by the discrete‑burst runners (VT, PS). When NaN (continuous SP/CP/LP) the first row instead reads “Capture #” = the capture index.
Cumulative pulse count (Cumulative Npulse) [count] Total pulses delivered up to and including this capture, accumulating over the run’s earlier captures (resets per channel/combo). Shown in the normal view (VT/PS only).
Cumulative charge (Cumulative Q) [nC, auto‑scaled nC/µC/mC] Cumulative cathodic charge delivered to the electrode so far = Σ |Qph,i| × Npulse,i (resets per channel/combo). Shown in the normal view (VT/PS only).
Fixed (scheduled) sample time (Fixed Time) [s] The cadence‑grid time (n × sampling interval, anchored at run start) this capture aimed for — the precise‑timing reference the periodic sampler targets regardless of per‑capture duration. Populated for the periodic runners (PS, LP); NaN for the adaptive VT ramp. Shown in the SUMMARY and POLARIS.
Elapsed (actual) sample time (Elapsed Time) [s] The actual measured elapsed time (monotonic, anchored at run start; for LP, pulsing time with pauses excluded) when this capture was taken — the counterpart to Fixed Time for reading scheduling jitter. Shown in the SUMMARY and POLARIS.
Time to complete channel/combo [s, shown m/h] Wall‑clock time to complete a whole channel/combo run (finished − started). Shown as the POLARIS “Time to complete” row and the Gamry electrode‑sheet ELAPSED entry; NaN until the run finishes.
KHFAC continuous‑sinusoidal (kilohertz AC)
Pulse frequency [kHz] The fundamental sinusoid frequency of a continuous‑sinusoidal (KHFAC) capture — the waveform’s rate is its frequency (labelled “pulse frequency”, not rate). Taken from the exact pattern rate. Shown in the KHFAC view.
Ghazavi access resistance (Raccess) [kΩ] For a continuous sinusoid, the access (electrolyte) resistance from the in‑phase least‑squares projection of the measured electrode voltage onto the current (Ghazavi & Cogan 2018, ideal‑capacitor assumption). The KHFAC electrode‑health metric. Reported for the active and return electrodes.
Ghazavi access voltage (Vaccess) [V] For a continuous sinusoid, the access‑voltage amplitude Vro = Raccess·Io — the resistive iR‑drop amplitude at peak current. Active and return.
Ghazavi interface polarization amplitude (Eio) [V] Half the peak‑to‑peak excursion of the de‑ohm’d interface potential Ei(t) = Vm − Raccess·I — the AC polarization amplitude of the electrode interface under continuous excitation (Eio = ½(Ema − Emc)). Active and return.
Ghazavi offset potential (Eoff) [V] The DC operating point of the interface under continuous excitation = the mean measured electrode potential over the capture. Active and return. (Emc = Eoff − Eio, Ema = Eoff + Eio.)
Phase angle (φImon / φVmon / φEret / φEact) [°] The impedance/EIS phase angle of each voltage waveform relative to Imon at the drive frequency (single‑bin lock‑in): ~0° purely resistive, →−90° purely capacitive (voltage lags current). Imon is the phase reference, so φImon = +0.0° by definition. Shown in the KHFAC view (the Imon anchor plus the finite voltage‑trace rows).
Pulse rate / pulse period (Pulse rate [pps] / Pulse period) The pulse repetition rate — pulses per second, labelled pps (never Hz for a pulse rate) — and its reciprocal period (auto‑scaled µs/ms/s). Shown in the normal and KHFAC views.
Galvanostatic EIS (impedance spectroscopy)
Complex impedance point (Z: |Z|, ∠Z, Zreal, Zimag) [Ω, °] For the Galvanostatic EIS experiment, the complex electrode impedance Z(f) at this capture’s probe frequency (one capture per swept frequency, single‑bin lock‑in Z = V/I): the magnitude |Z| [Ω], the phase ∠Z [°] (~0° resistive, →−90° capacitive), and the Nyquist coordinates Zreal / Zimag [Ω]. Plotted on the Bode and Nyquist sub‑tabs; NaN for non‑EIS experiments.

16 References

The metrics, safety limits, and analysis methods in PULSAR follow the established neural-stimulation electrode-characterization literature. The works below are the primary sources for the water window and charge-injection safety limits, the voltage-transient and chronopotentiometry methods PULSAR implements, and the sputtered-iridium-oxide (SIROF), activated-iridium-oxide (AIROF), and platinum electrode data against which results are interpreted.

Citing these in a manuscript. Digital object identifiers (DOIs) are given for every reference. Re-check each citation against the primary source (author list, volume, and page/article number) before using it in a formal publication.

16.1 Electrochemistry & safety limits

  1. Cogan SF. Neural stimulation and recording electrodes. Annual Review of Biomedical Engineering. 2008;10:275–309. doi:10.1146/annurev.bioeng.10.061807.160518. — The definitive review of electrode materials, the water window, and charge-injection limits; the basis for PULSAR’s reversible-charge-injection framing.
  2. Merrill DR, Bikson M, Jefferys JGR. Electrical stimulation of excitable tissue: design of efficacious and safe protocols. Journal of Neuroscience Methods. 2005;141(2):171–198. doi:10.1016/j.jneumeth.2004.10.020. — Reversible vs. irreversible charge injection and the design of charge-balanced biphasic protocols.
  3. Shannon RV. A model of safe levels for electrical stimulation. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. 1992;39(4):424–426. doi:10.1109/10.126616. — The charge / charge-density (k) safety boundary.
  4. McCreery DB, Agnew WF, Yuen TGH, Bullara L. Charge density and charge per phase as cofactors in neural injury induced by electrical stimulation. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. 1990;37(10):996–1001. doi:10.1109/10.102812. — The co-dependence of charge per phase and charge density in stimulation-induced neural injury.
  5. Merrill DR. The electrochemistry of charge injection at the electrode/tissue interface. In: Implantable Neural Prostheses 2: Techniques and Engineering Approaches. New York: Springer; 2010:85–138. doi:10.1007/978-0-387-98120-8_4. — Capacitive vs. Faradaic charge transfer at the electrode interface.

16.2 Voltage transients & chronopotentiometry

  1. Harris AR, Newbold C, Carter P, Cowan R, Wallace GG. Using chronopotentiometry to better characterize the charge injection mechanisms of platinum electrodes used in bionic devices. Frontiers in Neuroscience. 2019;13:380. doi:10.3389/fnins.2019.00380. — The total current is the sum of capacitive and Faradaic components (i = ic + if), so I / (dV/dt) from a pulse is not a true double-layer capacitance.
  2. Harris AR. Limitations in the electrochemical analysis of voltage transients. Journal of Neural Engineering. 2024;21(1):013003. doi:10.1088/1741-2552/ad1e23. — A voltage transient cannot cleanly separate the ohmic, capacitive, and Faradaic contributions; access, polarization, and driving quantities should be reported as voltages. This is why PULSAR reports voltages (and only reports an effective capacitance for the purely capacitive / open / broken cases).
  3. Harris AR, Newbold C, Carter P, Cowan R, Wallace GG. Measuring the effective area and charge density of platinum electrodes for bionic devices. Journal of Neural Engineering. 2018;15(4):046015. doi:10.1088/1741-2552/aaba8b. — The distinction between geometric and electrochemically active area when normalizing charge to charge density.
  4. Nguyen CK, Sturgill BS, Negi S, Cogan SF. Analyzing voltage transients under different stimulation configurations and rates in rat cortex. In: 2024 46th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC). 2024:1–4. doi:10.1109/EMBC53108.2024.10781825. — The voltage-transient method (access voltage/resistance, driving voltage, electrode polarization, Qph, max Qinj) that PULSAR implements.
  5. Nguyen CK, Azami A, Nguyen MA, Negi S, Cogan SF. Charge-injection comparison of SIROF-coated Utah electrode arrays across stimulation polarities, configurations, and patterns. In: 2025 12th International IEEE/EMBS Conference on Neural Engineering (NER). 2025 (in press). — SIROF Utah-array charge injection across stimulation polarity, configuration, and pattern — the parameters PULSAR is designed to sweep.

  2. Cogan SF, Guzelian AA, Agnew WF, Yuen TGH, McCreery DB. Over-pulsing degrades activated iridium oxide films used for intracortical neural stimulation. Journal of Neuroscience Methods. 2004;137(2):141–150. doi:10.1016/j.jneumeth.2004.02.019. — Why staying within the water window matters: exceeding the safe charge-injection limit degrades the electrode.

Biomedical Materials. 2010;5(1):015007. doi:10.1088/1748-6041/5/1/015007. — SIROF vs. platinum charge-injection performance (Solzbacher Laboratory).
  4. Frederick RA, Shih Y-C, Towle VL, Joshi-Imre A, Troyk PR, Cogan SF. Chronic stability of activated iridium oxide film voltage transients from wireless floating microelectrode arrays. Frontiers in Neuroscience. 2022;16:876032. doi:10.3389/fnins.2022.876032.

Extending the understanding of Shannon’s safe stimulation limit for platinum electrodes: biphasic charge-balanced pulse trains in unbuffered saline at pH 1 to pH 12. Journal of Neural Engineering. 2024;21(5):056007. doi:10.1088/1741-2552/ad3b6a.
